entries.title: Kevin Kiley Loses Reelection After California Redistricting
entries.summary: The lawmaker, a former Republican, became a top critic of redistricting in the House of Representatives.
entries.content:
The nationwide redistricting war has claimed one of its staunchest critics, with Republican-turned-independent Rep. Kevin Kiley projected to lose reelection in California’s newly redrawn 6th Congressional District.

Kiley became one of the most outspoken critics of redistricting in the House of Representatives as it became clear he might become a victim of it. He introduced legislation that would halt a burgeoning nationwide redistricting battle in August 2025 and a discharge petition in May that would force a vote on his bill — though his legislative push to end the redistricting war went nowhere.

“I spoke with Richard Pan and congratulated him on being elected to represent the 6th District,” he said on social media. “I'm proud of our campaign and grateful for the amazing support of so many people. Thank you for believing California is worth fighting for.”

After Texas’ move to gerrymander out five Democratic-held seats, California Democrats countered with Proposition 50, a ballot initiative which would effectively carve out as many new Democratic-leaning seats. Kiley excoriated gerrymandering anywhere as a “plague on our democracy.”

“This is insanity. Where does it end?” he asked on the House floor in September 2025, lamenting that “My own district, for example, under a newly proposed map, would be cut into six different pieces.”

Prop 50 passed in November 2025 with nearly two-thirds of the vote. Kiley then chose to run in a geographically smaller district that includes parts of Sacramento after his district was split six ways across the newly gerrymandered House map.

In March, he announced he had changed voter registration and party designation from Republican to independent, explaining in a House floor speech that he sought to be “an independent voice for the communities that I represent.”

Despite the switch, Kiley continued to support the Republican House majority on most party-line votes, but voted against the GOP’s second reconciliation bill.

He will be succeeded in Congress by Democrat Richard Pan, a pediatrician and former California state senator. He ran on a promise to stand up to President Donald Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., blasting their moves on health care and vaccines as harmful to families and children.

Kiley, who has only served in Congress since January 2023, was the House’s preeminent critic of California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

He wrote a 200-plus-page book titled “Recall Newsom” and ran for governor during the failed 2021 recall effort, placing sixth among the Newsom alternatives.

Kiley used the early months of Trump’s return to office to champion federal efforts that would curb California policy, including its status as a sanctuary state, its promotion of electric vehicles and its long-delayed high-speed rail program.

Across both his terms in Congress, Kiley introduced one bill that was signed into law: H.R. 9124 named a Veterans Affairs Clinic in his district after Lt. Cmdr.i Louis A. Conter, the last survivor of the USS Arizona.

entries.title: Inside the Republican Cataclysm
entries.summary: Interviews with more than 50 lawmakers, candidates, senior strategists and consultants from both parties reveal how Republicans walked into disaster — and how Democrats took advantage.
entries.content:
The election cycle had just started when Tim Scott, the newly elected chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, announced what his top priority was for the next two years.

It wasn’t defending the GOP’s Senate majority.

In one early 2025 meeting, Scott told Republicans that the most important thing to him is his relationship with President Donald Trump, three sources with knowledge of the comments told The Washington Sun. He added that he wouldn’t do anything as NRSC chair to jeopardize it, two of the sources said. It was an unusual statement from the Republican in charge of winning Senate races, who is normally expected to relentlessly advocate on behalf of his candidates.

Scott’s priority was shared across the Republican Party this year. It has now led Republicans to a historic electoral disaster.

Republicans suffered a cataclysmic wipeout Tuesday, a blowout many in Washington considered unthinkable in an era of hardened voter partisanship. The staggering volume of losses — at least 25 seats in the House and 7 in the Senate — matched the shock of how deeply Democrats reached into Trump territory, flipping MAGA-heavy districts where neither party committee spent a dime. Democrats swept to victory in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, snapping decades-old dry spells and elevating history-making candidates in places like Wisconsin, Georgia and Michigan.
Election 2026 Texas Senate (6915x4610, AR: 1.50)Election 2026 Kansas Senate (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)And at the heart of it all was Trump and a party congenitally unable to show independence from him. As the president’s approval sank to record lows — particularly for his handling of the economy, voters’ number one issue — party members stubbornly refused to put any distance between themselves and their leader, even when their own evidence suggested they should try. Reanimating the Trump 2024 coalition — held together by a populist streak that wrangled Latino, working-class and young voters — failed miserably.

The writing had been on the wall for months. When Republicans decamped Washington this past winter for a private retreat in Florida, they got a five-alarm warning from Chris Winkelman, who leads the Congressional Leadership Fund, the flagship House GOP super PAC. He told lawmakers in a briefing at the March meeting that the midterms, then eight months away, were a growing problem.

“It is entirely possible that we're going to lose 10 incumbents,” he told the members, according to two people who were in the room.

By Tuesday night, it was clear that Winkelman’s warning was not nearly dire enough.

GOP pollster Robert Blizzard said “the Trump coalition came apart at the seams.” Mike DuHaime, the former political director of the Republican National Committee, called it “a Watergate-level loss.” Longtime North Carolina GOP strategist Paul Shumaker said that Trump voters “feel betrayed.”

One Republican operative called it a “total ass-kicking from coast to coast” that laid at the feet of the president and his political team. A second called it an “absolute embarrassment" for party leaders like Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Campaign Committee, who saw all of their strategies “blow up in their faces.”
Trump (8287x5525, AR: 1.50)Interviews with more than 50 lawmakers, candidates, senior strategists and consultants from both parties, some of whom were granted anonymity to share internal party deliberations, reveal how Republicans blundered their way into a cataclysmic loss that leaves the future viability of MAGA in doubt and resuscitates a Democratic Party that looked nearly dead two years ago.

And they showed the startling miscalculation of a party that devised a strategy almost singularly focused on embracing Trump, even as evidence mounted that the public backlash against him was the most severe a president had faced in decades.

A spokesperson for the NRSC called the account of Scott’s remarks “categorically false and a 1000% lie.”

Republicans’ Big Redistricting Flop 

Republicans started the cycle in 2025 with a risky gambit to keep the map in their favor: mid-decade redistricting. Led by White House political adviser James Blair, Republicans leaned on red-state governors and legislators to redraw their congressional maps to pad the party’s margins ahead of what has historically been a tough midterm political environment.

The line-moving — which started in Texas in July 2025 — put 22 Democratic incumbents into districts Trump won in 2024, up from 13 at the beginning of the cycle. But by Tuesday night, of the seven red states that redrew their districts, aiming to pick up up to 15 seats, Republicans did not appear to be on track to win any of them. In Texas, Democrats smothered GOP candidates in the Rio Grande Valley, a redistricting hot spot.

“The undertow of the national wave will reach deeper in Texas than anywhere else, and D.C. operatives never accounted for that in their math,” said a Texas GOP consultant. “The genius idea a few D.C. operatives had to redraw the congressional map [is now] laughable.”

But last year, when redistricting still looked like a daring move, Democrats were caught flat-footed. They “didn’t have a game plan,” said Will Van Nuys, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s deputy executive director. That didn’t last.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom quickly floated the idea of redrawing his own state, after his team figured out if it was “legally feasible, politically feasible” to pass a ballot initiative to overturn the state’s independent, commission-drawn lines, said a person familiar with Newsom’s thinking. They added: “This all started with Gavin.”
Redistricting Blue States (3785x2524, AR: 1.50)By August 2025, Democratic leadership gathered over Zoom on the sidelines of a major donor retreat at the Torrey Pines Golf Course in San Diego to discuss whether they would counter Texas with a California redraw. Representatives for Newsom, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the DCCC and the House Majority PAC decided to give it the green light, according to two people involved in the discussions.

“Gavin's going to have to put his neck on the line and potentially ruin his presidential chances if we lost,” said Mike Smith, president of House Majority PAC. “And I think it was all making a blood pact that we're not letting this down.”

California’s vote count is still trickling in, but Democrats could pick up up to five additional seats in the state. The move will buoy Newsom as he eyes a 2028 presidential run.

Democrats thought they’d hit another wall when the party’s efforts to redraw the lines in Virginia were thrown out by the state’s Supreme Court. A senior NRCC official was in a meeting with congressional chiefs of staff when his phone wouldn’t stop buzzing on the wooden conference-room table. When he announced to the room that the court had blocked the Democratic-drawn seats, the room broke out into cheers.

The brief victory, though, just clouded deeper problems in the Republican ranks.

The Struggle to Recruit Candidates

When Scott met with Gov. Brian Kemp in Atlanta in April 2025, it was ostensibly to recruit the popular governor into challenging Sen. Jon Ossoff. The race, one of the GOP’s few clear offensive opportunities this cycle, was expected to be the most expensive and competitive race in the country. Recruiting Kemp would be a coup for Republicans.

But Scott did not effectively sell Kemp on the Senate, according to two people briefed on the interaction, even though he promised Kemp enormous financial backing. Instead, Scott told the governor that he wasn’t long for the Senate himself, one of those people said.

“If you had said to him, ‘We’ll get you on Foreign Relations and Armed Services, you can talk to generals, travel around the world’ — he’s a Bush foreign policy guy; he’s got a lot of interest in foreign policy, and he would’ve been really intrigued,” said the second person with direct knowledge of the interaction. “Kemp was open, but it was a lackluster, unimpressive effort. As soon as they failed to get Kemp, that race was over.”
Trump (5686x3791, AR: 1.50)Republicans, in private, didn’t limit the blame to Scott. Trump’s meddling in Senate primaries triggered enormous frustration in some corners of the party, especially his endorsements of the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister. Both lost Tuesday night.

He also backed former RNC Chair Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia, who proved disappointing. GOP super PACs ultimately cut off spending in both states this fall — states that operatives in both parties expected a year ago to be at the center of the political universe.

“He’s an incredible salesman to his own people, but his deficit is the bully pulpit and being able to explain to the middle of the electorate what he’s done,” a senior GOP operative said of Trump.

But, this operative added, “the Republican Party has gotten lazy. They get a Trump endorsement and that’s all they run on.”

Dialing into Fox News early Wednesday morning, Trump was defiant. When asked about “candidate quality” and if he had regrets, he said, “I had no choice.”

Democrats had their own tumultuous primaries, but they were able to limit the ultimate damage. In Maine, Graham Platner easily defeated Chuck Schumer’s handpicked candidate, Gov. Janet Mills, before he was forced to abandon the race after he was accused of sexually assaulting a woman.

The accusation’s appearance in the media wasn’t a coincidence: Democratic operatives in Washington, convinced that rumors of Platner’s sexual misconduct would eventually emerge and sink his campaign against Collins, worked behind the scenes to make sure any such story was published before the July 15 ballot deadline, according to two people with knowledge of the effort. “If that story had come out even eight days later, we would have been stuck with him,” one of the sources said.

Democrats ultimately held a summer convention and picked Troy Jackson to replace Platner on the ballot, likely saving the seat for the party. Jackson defeated Collins on Tuesday.

How Democrats Pushed Back Against Republicans’ Cash Advantage

The nagging fear for many Democrats working congressional races was their bank accounts.

Quarter after quarter, the Republican ecosystem grew its pool of cash, while Democrats struggled mightily to keep up, particularly with donors who cut big checks. The problem for Democrats multiplied this summer with a Supreme Court case that opened up coordination between the committees and campaigns. The RNC, MAGA Inc. and other GOP-backed super PACs flooded the landscape with cash, which would eventually crack ad-spending records for a midterm cycle.

In mid-July, one day after the Supreme Court lifted those coordination limits, GOP members in the NRCC’s Patriot Program met with the NRCC chair and executive director. One Republican member pressed for more financial help from the committee. A person inside the room remembered afterward: “And I was like, ‘Wow, oh, that's legal now.’”

By late summer, Democrats started to raise private, and increasingly public, alarms over the disparity and whether it’d hamper the party’s efforts to expand deeper into GOP territory. Days after House Speaker Mike Johnson met with GOP megadonor Elon Musk in late August about his own midterm spending, Van Nuys knew the DCCC had to get creative.
Trump AI (5703x3802, AR: 1.50)Following a Saturday Zoom meeting before Labor Day, when Van Nuys realized the DCCC was defending more seats than it was pushing into, he decided to pitch an unprecedented way to save the committee some much-needed cash. He proposed putting 13 Democratic members, who represented the second tier of front-line districts, into a weekly polling program to track their races. Then, move all the cash earmarked for those incumbents into offensive House races deeper into the GOP battlefield. The DCCC’s executive director, Julie Merz, pitched it directly to members days later.

That move, internally called the “Polling Protection Program,” freed up nearly $10 million, Van Nuys said, for races like those in Iowa’s 2nd District and Texas’ 35th. By early Wednesday morning, Democrats had flipped both.

The high-dollar checks did come — they just came at the end, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg pumped $84 million, as did Future Forward, the flagship super PAC behind Kamala Harris’ 2024 election, with $77 million.

For some Democrats, the tide was so high that the cash was unnecessary. In North Carolina, riding on Democrat Roy Cooper’s coattails, Cyril Jefferson didn’t spend any cash on ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, but he beat Republican Rep. Addison McDowell, who spent about $230,000.

“The money has failed. Redistricting has failed. Them hitting us on trans or defund the police or tying us to communism, all of that has failed,” Van Nuys said in an interview with The Sun in October. “No matter what they throw at us in the next few weeks, I feel very confident in where we stand right now.”

Republicans Stuck Close to Trump

By the end of spring, Democrats started to see signs that they were on track for a big year.

One senior House Democratic operative recounted seeing a poll in mid-June of Arizona’s battleground 6th Congressional District, where political newcomer JoAnna Mendoza was taking on Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani. Mendoza’s name ID was barely above 30%, but she still led Ciscomani by 2 percentage points on an early ballot test.

It would be the start of a flurry of internal Democratic polling that showed numbers so positive that many operatives struggled to believe them.

“We had just never seen polling this good,” the senior Democratic strategist said. “It’s hard to be excited when you see one good poll. But when you never see any negative polls, it’s a ‘holy shit, something is happening here’ moment.”

There was little doubt why Democrats were starting to see especially favorable data at the start of summer: The Iran war and its effect on gas prices was torpedoing Republicans. Trump starting a new war, despite promising to end them, and heating up inflation, after promising to tame it, left the Republican base deflated. While Republicans hoped the Iran operation would be a short-lived intervention akin to the targeted operation in Venezuela earlier that year, the United States has spent nearly all of 2026 engaged in occasional skirmishes. The Trump administration conducted defensive strikes on Iran the day before the election. Nationally, gas prices average $4.15 a gallon, compared to $2.98 before the war.

It was the "reverse Dobbs effect," a senior GOP national strategist said in describing the Iran war’s impact on the GOP base. In 2022, the Supreme Court overturned abortion rights in its Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization decision, which injected energy into a depressed Democratic base and led to the party faring better than expected.

Even if Trump’s popularity was starting to dip, most Republican candidates still showed little interest in distancing themselves from their party or its leader. Republican political operatives have long resisted breaking with Trump, convinced that doing so would do more to depress turnout in the MAGA base than win over swing voters. They explicitly decided to double down on the strategy this election cycle, confident they could persuade many of the Trump supporters who usually skip midterm elections to turn out this year.
Trump (8345x5563, AR: 1.50)But by the start of 2026, Trump had already become more unpopular than he had at almost any previous point in his tenure. It wouldn't get any better from there.

By the time this summer arrived, Trump’s popularity had already taken a significant hit in public polling because of the Iran war, according to polls. Some GOP strategists concluded that putting a little distance between their candidates and the president was becoming a political necessity.

“It’s just truthful that he is the most unpopular president we’ve had in a long time,” said one senior GOP strategist. “More unpopular than Biden was.”

Republicans had both big and small opportunities to distance themselves from Trump, GOP officials said, whether over Iran or when the president attempted to rename one of the Great Lakes. But almost until the end, any such effort never materialized.

“We failed to do it,” retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said. “We became a department of the executive branch, and it didn't work. It never does. Didn't work for Obama. Didn't work for Trump, politically."

Tillis underscored a war powers resolution over the summer as proof of the pressure Republicans felt to toe the administration’s line on Iran, saying that the White House was whipping the position even though the resolution was effectively meaningless.

“I mean, that was the level of control that they've exerted over the conference to our own disadvantage,” the North Carolina Republican said. “There's no separation. There's only barely. People are saying, ‘Well, we're not, I'm not happy with what's going on with the war.’”

Some Senate Republican strategists were especially distressed by Scott’s stance. They believed Scott, in his formal role, should be responsible for convincing Trump that the party’s candidates need to show some measure of dissent on issues like tariffs and the war. They quickly came to believe he was unwilling to do that. That left them fearful that if they spoke out, they could expect an attack from Trump and little to no backup from the NRSC.

“They thought of it as their job to represent the White House’s view to the Senate candidates, not the other way around,” said the senior GOP strategist, who suggested that a candidate like Ashley Hinson should have been given the green light over the summer to start forcefully opposing the tariffs because of the particularly harmful effect they’ve had on farmers.

“We don’t fucking do persausion anymore,” the strategist continued. “We’re just going to say the base-motivating thing over and over again. And that’s a big problem. There was no effort to help campaigns with what those persuasive swing-voter messages were.”

Scott defenders dispute that the senator didn’t stand up for Republican candidates to Trump, pointing out that he backed Cornyn over Paxton and helped engineer a temporary tariff freeze. He also publicly criticized a Truth Social post of Trump’s from last year

“Chairman Scott took the job as NRSC Chair knowing that it would lead to conflicts with the White House, including tireless defense of incumbents like John Cornyn,” an NRSC spokesperson said.

By the time summer ended, Republicans felt relatively confident about the state of the midterm map. The environment was rough, but many of their candidates in key House and Senate races were still competitive.

Republicans’ Fall Panic

Republicans had just wrapped their midterm convention in Dallas where Trump begged Republicans to pretend he was on the ballot. The economy and the Iran war, the 100-pound weights around the party’s necks, were ignored. After a tough August, when their candidates languished in the low 40s in internal polling, Republican strategists and operatives expected their voters would return to their partisan corners, as they traditionally have in recent cycles.
Mike Rogers,Tim Scott (5314x3543, AR: 1.50)APTOPIX Trump (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)By mid-September, they started to realize it wasn’t going to work out that way.

A flurry of Republican polls one week after the convention showed a precipitous drop across the board for the party. Trump’s image dropped, candidates once sporting a significant lead fell back into statistical dead-heats and a map that looked competitive when the month began was suddenly tilting quickly to the left.

“That was the point at which, OK, we've got to hunker down and now go all in and make sure that we maintain the Senate,” said Alex Latcham, president of the Senate Leadership Fund, the flagship Senate GOP super PAC. “This is no longer about picking up seats.”

Despite a barrage of negative ads against Democrats, “no matter what you did, voters were just not fucking listening,” another Republican strategist said. “And you can’t break through. And it just got tougher and tougher.”

Republicans’ nerves mirrored Democrats’ disbelief.

Democrats’ biggest problem, in fact, might have been managing the sheer number of good polls Democratic operatives were seeing internally: One official with the House Majority PAC said campaigns were constantly clamoring for the super PAC to release data about their race, faster than the group was actually able to release them.

Leading Democratic strategists said the game plan this year was simple: focus on economic issues, push as deeply as they could into red territory and hope that Republicans keep focusing on the culture-war issues that dominated most of their advertising, like the party’s relentless focus on transgender issues.

Their only confusion was why Republicans remained so confident about the state of the map late in election season.

“I always assume the other side knows what they are doing. But over the last 18 months, it became increasingly obvious they didn’t,” said Ian Russell, a Democratic strategist. “From ‘Liberation Day’ to the ‘big, beautiful bill’ to attacking Iran — just one unforced error after another.”

Some Republicans agreed.

“Even though they voted for Trump in 2024, he’s doing everything but what he said he’s going to do,” said Shumaker, the North Carolina-based GOP consultant. “That coalition he had was created, in large part, by Joe Biden and Kamala Harris’ failure on the economy. Why should anybody think they will maintain that coalition without focusing on the economy?”

How Far the Map Went

When state Rep. Lindsay James, a chaplain, launched her congressional run in Iowa, few Democrats thought she had a chance.

“There was a lot of dismissing this race in particular,” James said in late October, during a break from greeting Grinnell College students during early voting. She said she’d heard from Democratic donors, consultants and activists: “It’s too hard, it’s too red, it’s too far gone.” And she worried “Democrats have left the Midwest behind.”

She noticed a shift on the ground this summer, as she held a 22-county town-hall tour, when not just Democratic activists but also Republicans and independents started showing up. When Van Nuys, the DCCC deputy executive director, cooked up the plan to free up cash in early September, one of the top districts the committee wanted to jump into was James’ — a district Trump won by 10 points.

By late October, after significant spending on both sides, James led GOP state Rep. Joe Mitchell by an 8-point margin, according to the DCCC’s internal tracking numbers. As James hugged Grinnell students who told her they’d voted for her, she surveyed them on what snacks her congressional office should stock when she was elected.

James ultimately beat Mitchell on Tuesday night. She’s clear-eyed about what Democrats must do to hold onto these voters, who are primarily angry about Trump but haven’t bought into the Democratic Party, either.
Election 2026 Rural Democrats (3785x2524, AR: 1.50)“Any kind of political theater, I’m not interested in that,” James said. She warned of potential distractions, like another Trump impeachment. “We need to deliver, and we need to deliver quickly.”

In the final days of the campaign, James traded messages on a particularly active Signal thread, composed of 14 of the DCCC’s Red to Blue women candidates. It was a place to lean on each other for advice because “there’s challenges for women candidates that are unique,” she said.

Denise Powell, who flipped an Omaha-based district Tuesday night, has taken to sending each of her fellow candidates in the Signal chat friendship bracelets, à la Taylor Swift, in the lead up to Election Day. James’ bracelet has messages like “Vote for Lindsay” and “Fiery Redhead.”

Good luck charms, James said. It’s luck those Democratic candidates didn’t end up needing.

entries.title: Democrats Are Already Feuding Over the Meaning of the Midterms
entries.summary: Progressives say the wins mean the party must fight Trump harder, while moderates say focus on the economy.
entries.content:
The votes haven’t been fully counted yet in the 2026 midterm elections, but Democrats are already clashing over the meaning of the results, which saw the party sweep control of both the House and Senate in a major rebuke to President Donald Trump.

Progressive and centrist Democrats alike won in red districts and red states across the country, making inroads with virtually every demographic group. The makeup of Democrats’ new Senate majority next year will include several progressives like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, who ran on single-payer health care and abolishing the filibuster, and centrists like Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, who are opposed to both.

But progressive lawmakers and advocates argue that Tuesday’s results demand a more aggressive posture against Trump in the new Democratic-led Congress, including ramping up investigations of alleged corruption in his administration, fighting harder against mass deportation and strict immigration policies, and denying funding to the Iran war.

Reacting to news of Democrats winning control of the Senate in a post online, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar (Texas) urged the Senate to abolish the filibuster next year in order to pass progressive legislation. Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has warned that Democrats may fail to capture the White House in 2028 if they don’t show voters they are on their side.

Other progressives urged Democrats to engage in even more hardball tactics.

“Tonight, voters ended Trump's Republican trifecta and his blank check. They also closed the book on a Democratic Party that folds when it counts," Ezra Levin, co-executive director of Indivisible, said in a statement. "For too long, Democratic leaders treated caving as strategy, from walking away from the shutdown fight empty-handed to waving through Trump's nominees. That era is over.”

“Democrats now hold the gavels in both chambers, and for the first time they'll have a bloc of fighters inside both caucuses pushing them to use them. Voters didn't flip Congress for polite hearings and strongly worded letters,” Levin added.

Meanwhile, Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, spun Democrat James Talarico’s huge victory over Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race as a win for progressive messaging around economic populism.

"James Talarico just showed Democrats how to win in Texas by consistently challenging billionaire power, calling out Wall Street and Big Tech, and calling for bold structural change,” Green said in a statement. “Political insiders have spent months debating whether Talarico is a ‘moderate’ or a ‘progressive,’ and they’re missing the point. He ran as an economic populist who promised to shake up a broken system, and as a person of faith with a moral obligation to challenge corporate greed.”

Polls showed the economy and corruption as the top two issues in this election. Most Democrats ran on ending Trump’s war in Iran and bringing down the high costs of gas, health care and consumer goods. They also vowed to crack down on allegations of self-dealing and corruption in Trump’s administration.

Top Democratic officials have sought to tamp down aspirations about passing far-reaching progressive legislation while Trump remains in the White House, stressing Democrats would focus instead on addressing affordability issues, ending the Iran war and reversing Republican cuts to health care.

“We got to govern,” Sen. Mark Kelly (Arizona), a potential 2028 presidential contender, told The Washington Sun on a press call on Tuesday night. “We've got to deliver for the American people. And you guys know how it works in the Senate — we got to get Republicans on board with some of the stuff we want to do. So it's got to be somewhat bipartisan. We got to send legislation to the president's desk.”

Asked about progressive calls to fight Trump harder and the possibility of another House impeachment of Trump next year, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer also seemed to dismiss the idea Tuesday night.

"Our number one focus has to be producing for the American people in terms of their number one need, the high costs that Trump has imposed on them, and second, to go after the corruption,” Schumer told The Sun at a press conference outside the headquarters of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at the centrist think tank Third Way and a former senior aide to Schumer, said Tuesday’s results are “a spectacular night for moderate Democrats,” who flipped seats in red states like Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina.

He also sought to portray El-Sayed’s win over Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, a race that was closer than Democrats initially expected, as the result of a favorable environment for Democrats nationwide, rather than any kind of verdict for advancing more progressive policies, as some progressive advocates have argued.

“In a normal year, in a neutral year, El-Sayed probably doesn't win Michigan,” Kessler argued. “He's getting a boost. But in the places where we're having shocking outcomes, these Democrats are moderate.”

With Democrats overperforming across the board on Tuesday, it will be difficult for either intraparty faction to claim a mandate for their preferred policy outcomes, but the debate is likely to rage on into the new Congress.

“Everyone got wins here, because we did it as a big tent and a family,” one national Democratic operative told The Sun.

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Wins Michigan, Hanging On to a Battleground Seat for Democrats
entries.summary: The progressive Democrat beat Trump-backed Mike Rogers in an open race that drew national attention and big spending.
entries.content:
DETROIT — Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to win the open U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, marking a potentially pivotal moment for his party after an ugly election cycle.

Progressives nationally bet big on El-Sayed, arguing for months that a candidate on the left could win in a swing state like Michigan by focusing on economic issues with a boisterous political and personal style. His victory gives his ideological allies — including dedicated endorsers like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) — a potent claim on where the Democratic Party goes from here.

El-Sayed called himself the “unlikeliest” of candidates and said Rogers ran “one of the ugliest campaigns we’ve seen in our lifetimes” at his watch party in Detroit.

“The opposition decided to try to divide us,” El-Sayed said. “At first, they pointed to my name and my faith, as if to say, ‘You know, he’s a little different’ … but we all know my name and my faith aren’t the reason you can’t afford your gas.”

The seat was expected to be key in deciding control of the Senate, but by the time the race was called Democrats had long since won control, making El-Sayed’s win more of a buffer than a linchpin for Democrats.

A tired but ecstatic crowd at El-Sayed’s party on election night cheered as the Michigan Democrat proclaimed victory from the stage shortly before 2 a.m. ET, before the race had been called. Members of the United Auto Workers, an influential labor union in Michigan that backed El-Sayed, hugged after he left the stage.

The campaign was caught up in drama in its final days, as Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary, announced a surprise endorsement of Mike Rogers, the Republican in the race — a reversal from her previous support for El-Sayed.

Her shift drew fury from other Democrats, who had largely rallied around El-Sayed in the months after the primary and were incensed that the primary’s loser could help hand the seat to Republicans. El-Sayed’s campaign pulled in a record $2.4 million in fundraising on the same day of Stevens’ announcement.

"It's a betrayal of everything that she said that she believes in,” Curtis Hertel, chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, told The Sun on Sunday. “At the end of the day, the betrayal to the party is one thing. The betrayal to her constituents is a much bigger deal.”

El-Sayed will be the first Muslim U.S. senator.
Election 2026 Michigan (7413x4942, AR: 1.50)The race was among the most competitive — and nastiest — in this year’s midterms. President Donald Trump, who was backing Rogers, called El-Sayed a “jihadist,” while Rogers and others accused him of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has disavowed the group.

El-Sayed and Rogers loudly and regularly attacked each other personally, whether it was El-Sayed questioning Rogers’ masculinity or Rogers comparing El-Sayed to a “glitchy AI chatbot.”

Stevens, in endorsing Rogers, focused on the fact that El-Sayed had disinvited her from his campaign events.

El-Sayed, a former public health official who won a grueling primary, focused much of his messaging on expanding Medicare coverage for all Americans and keeping corporate interests out of politics.

He was buoyed by public frustration over the affordability crisis and Trump, especially as gas and diesel prices rose to near record highs in Michigan. Rogers sought to distance himself from some of the president’s policies. He objected to new tariffs on Canadian goods and called for an end to the Iran war.

“He’s going to make this about him and me,” El-Sayed said of Rogers during their first debate, in October. “But really, it’s about you and whether you can afford your gas and your groceries.”

El-Sayed won his primary by only 1 percentage point against Stevens in a race dominated by an intraparty split over strategy and U.S.-Israel relations.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee and its affiliated groups spent a record $30 million supporting Stevens in the primary. AIPAC announced in late October that it planned to spend as much as $9 million more to defeat El-Sayed in the general election.

Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) threw themselves into campaigning for El-Sayed during the primary, giving him national progressive shine and helping to push him to victory.

Susan Fabrick, the Democratic Party chair in Muskegon County, told The Washington Sun that although there was division in her swing county during the primary, most voters were able to come together to support El-Sayed in the general election.

“The Black community here was fairly strongly behind Haley Stevens,” she said. “But I had people come in the day after the primary and say, ‘We’re going to make sure Abdul wins.’ These were people who had supported somebody else.”

entries.title: Democrats Blow Out Republicans in Historic Midterm, Now Face Pressure to Deliver
entries.summary: A stinging rebuke of Donald Trump now points toward a clash with Republicans and within the party.
entries.content:
Democrats delivered a generational shellacking to Republicans in the midterm elections, flipping House and Senate majorities by winning in even some of the most conservative-leaning regions of the nation.

Riding a wave against President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war, Democrats won well beyond their coastal strongholds. They defeated GOP candidates and incumbents with diverse candidates in Midwest battlegrounds like Michigan and Ohio, and they made historic gains in deeply conservative states like Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

Their congressional margins are projected to far exceed what they reached in the 2006 and 2018 elections, the last two times they bounced back from grueling presidential losses to gain big in the following midterm elections. Their stunning victories served as an immediate rebalancing of power in a Washington that had grown accustomed to the Republican-led Congress rolling over to Trump’s wishes.

“In the north, in the south, in the east, in the west, in the midwest, from sea to shining sea, the American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption. They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told a Democratic crowd late Tuesday on Capitol Hill.

Jeffries is on track to make history as the first Black House speaker in early January when the 120th Congress is sworn in.

In those previous midterm victories, 2006 and 2018, Democrats governed on Capitol Hill with a deft hand that kept their liberal base energized and helped coax middle-of-the-road voters to trust their party’s next presidential nominee.

Ahead of Tuesday’s sweeping victories, Democrats started angling to determine how much credit various factions of their coalition deserve and how aggressively to pursue an investigative agenda focused on Trump.

Veterans of those past victories want their party to tailor its agenda toward centrist voters with highly focused legislation to combat inflation and corruption, believing that will set them up for another so-called trifecta victory such as they claimed in 2008 and 2020.

“Republicans will lose this election, but what Democrats do in 2027 will determine if we truly win,” Rahm Emanuel, who chaired the House Democratic political committee in 2006, told The Washington Sun. The former Chicago mayor, who might run for the 2028 presidential nomination, suggested that Democratic victories in significantly Trump-leaning states served as the most significant markers for the party’s future, not wins by candidates aligned with democratic socialists.

But in an election eve memo, the political arm of the Congressional Progressive Caucus argued that the party’s far-left energy in the primary season in safe liberal districts and swing states translated to wins across the country. These lawmakers want a full-combat approach against Trump, even a potential third impeachment, to reward party activists who supported their preferred candidates.

“The significance of blue-seat primaries should not be ignored, particularly when candidates overcome enormous odds. Democrats disregard their base at their own peril,” Evan Brown, the top aide for the CPC PAC, wrote in the memo.

Democrats expect to hold the largest House majority in a decade and help Jeffries avoid the perils of the last three speakers, who governed with such narrow margins that small ideological factions could hold their agenda hostage.
Midterm Elections (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)This result marks just the third time in 70 years that the president’s party lost control of both the House and Senate in the same election. In a particularly embarrassing moment, the House Republican campaign chief, Rep. Richard Hudson, was trailing his little-known challenger in his rural North Carolina seat after spending much of his time in recent weeks campaigning and fundraising for other GOP candidates across the nation.

And Democrats were on the verge of securing a majority of the nation’s 50 governorships for the first since 2010, while flipping control of state legislatures in key states such as Michigan and Texas.

Trump's political record has been mixed, going two for three in his own presidential campaigns, but his party has performed terribly in midterm elections when he is not on the ballot. Ahead of the 2016 elections, Republicans held 247 seats in the House — a figure that went mostly downhill during his decade of dominance. They are likely to fall below 200 House seats for the first time since 2010.

In early 2025, Democrats looked back to their 2018 victorious midterm for insight, when the Republican tax cut plan proved unpopular and their attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act backfired. That helped energize an exodus of Republican support in dozens of suburban districts, with the well-educated, professional classes moving sharply toward Democrats and powering a 41-seat gain to win the House majority.

Sure enough, by July 4, 2025, the Republicans had passed their lone legislative achievement of the 119th Congress: a massive policy bill that extended tax breaks to corporations and the wealthy, while eliminating health benefits for millions who rely on Medicaid.

Then Democrats rolled the dice in the fall and forced a six-week shutdown of the government in an attempt to extend tax breaks for working families to get ACA benefits. They eventually surrendered but had won a clear political victory pinning the loss of tax credits on Republicans.

But by early this year the climate shifted into something more similar to the 2006 midterms, when voters recoiled against the Bush administration’s handling of the Iraq war.

Trump’s tariffs and his decision to launch a war against Iran sent everyday expenses like gasoline and groceries soaring, while also crippling the farm economy.

“It’s very much a change election,” New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, told The Sun.

Gillibrand learned all about those types of elections 20 years ago, when Emanuel recruited her to run in a Republican-dominated district around Albany, leading to being part of a 30-seat wave that handed Democrats the majority that year. Sen. Charles E. Schumer, now the minority leader who found himself under steady criticism this year from liberal activists who considered him a relic of the past, sat at the helm of the DSCC back in 2006.
Kirsten Gillibrand (5045x3364, AR: 1.50)Health care access got folded into the broader “affordability” matrix this cycle, while Gillibrand and Schumer set out to recruit unique candidates that fit culturally conservative states like Iowa and Kansas.

“They were the best candidate for their state, and they were great,” Schumer told reporters late Tuesday, adding that Republicans stuck close to Trump on politically toxic positions. “Republicans made a choice and followed Trump over the cliff.”

Trump continued making decisions and comments that insulted voters, particularly his own supporters when he called the affordability issue “a hoax.”

“He’s laughing at them,” Gillibrand said.

Emanuel, who left Congress after the 2008 elections to become Barack Obama’s first White House chief of staff, said that voter attitudes toward George W. Bush in 2006 and Trump in 2026 had a key difference.

In reelecting Bush in 2004, barely two years after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, voters knew they were supporting a president focused on foreign policy, they just ended up upset with his handling of the war. In sending Trump back to the Oval Office, voters wanted no more wars and a laser focus on fighting inflation.

“In 2006, people were tired and upset. In 2026, people are angry,” Emanuel said.

Some Democrats are already calling for the most dramatic showdowns possible with Trump. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, for example, wants to extend funding for federal agencies into early next year instead of the full fiscal year.

This would allow Democrats to hold funding for the Iran war hostage, Van Hollen told The Sun’s Igor Bobic last week. “My view is we should not appropriate one penny for this illegal war in Iran, and we should not retroactively fund the illegal war in Iran.”

That would risk a federal government shutdown, the type of tactic that, in 2007 and 2008, then House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid avoided in trying to end the Iraq war.

And in 2019 Pelosi brushed back liberal demands to impeach Trump over accusations related to the 2016 campaign, only to agree to those proceedings when her moderate, swing-district Democrats called for hearings over his pressure campaign against Ukraine.

Even then, Pelosi managed to cut deals with Trump on North American trade, the federal budget and several bills in 2020 that pumped trillions of dollars into the pandemic-crippled economy.

Gillibrand believes Democratic candidates, from centrists like Adam Hamilton in Kansas to far-left liberals like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, support cost-of-living issues like trying to end tariffs and the Iran war, and reducing the cost of prescription drugs — and they can avoid bitter fights that divide the party.

“I think there’s enough common ground,” she said.
Adam Hamilton (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Emanuel suggested threading the needle by moving quickly with legislation to raise the minimum wage, fight government corruption and affordability items in the first few weeks of the new Congress.

A fast-moving agenda would appeal to the activist base and put Republicans in a jam over supporting the popular items.

Schumer echoed that sentiment.

“Our number one focus has to be producing for the American people in terms of their number one need, the high costs that Trump has imposed on them, and second, to go after the corruption. This is the most corrupt administration in American history,” he told reporters.

entries.title: Democrat Elaine Luria Defeats Incumbent in Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District
entries.summary: Luria served two terms in the House before losing to Republican Jen Kiggans in 2022.
entries.content: Democrat Elaine Luria won election Tuesday to the U.S. House of Representatives representing Virginia's 2nd Congressional District, defeating Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans. Luria served two terms in the House before losing to Kiggans in 2022. During her time in Congress, she served on the committee that investigate the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Before her first stint in the House, she served in the Navy for two decades, reaching the rank of commander. Kiggans is also a Navy veteran who has served two terms in the House. The Associated Press declared Luria the winner at 11:47 p.m. EST.

entries.title: One Pennsylvania Republican Hugged Trump, Another Shunned Him. They Both Lost
entries.summary: Two Republican incumbents in Pennsylvania took starkly different approaches to messaging about Trump on the campaign trail.
entries.content:
As Republican incumbents in purple Pennsylvania battled strong political headwinds this November, they were forced to choose a tack –– hew closely to President Donald Trump or go their own way.

The question loomed large as the president’s approval rating continued to sink in the state –– one late-October poll showed 70% of Pennsylvania voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance.

Two of the battleground state’s longest-serving Republican incumbents –– Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry –– chose opposite courses on the campaign trail this fall. It didn't make a difference as Democrats swept in deep red districts across the country, including in areas that Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Fitzpatrick, who distanced himself from the increasingly unpopular president and his war in Iran, was projected to lose his seat in the 1st Congressional District to Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie.

Perry, who stuck by Trump and defended some of the administration’s most controversial moves while serving his seventh term in Congress, was also projected to lose to the Democratic nominee, former local news anchor Janelle Stelson, in his Harrisburg-area district.

In Pennsylvania, Republicans lost all four of their most contested districts — in Pennsylvania’s 8th District, Rep. Rob Bresnahan was projected to lose his seat to Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti after drawing criticism for his stock trading in a year when voters were angry about corruption. Over in the Lehigh Valley’s 7th Congressional District, Rep. Ryan Mackenzie was also projected to lose against the Democrat nominee, firefighter Bob Brooks.

The loss of Pennsylvania’s four competitive districts alongside an over 20-point win for Democratic Gov.Josh Shapiro could cement a new direction for the state, where those districts have historically swung back and forth between the two political parties.

The moderate Fitzpatrick had represented Republicans’ best hope in the state in a wave election year for Democrats. He represented his suburban community for 10 years, after winning the seat of his late brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, and criticized the president’s tariff policies, his comments on Russia’s war in Ukraine, and the administration’s proposed “anti-weaponization” fund. He voted to end hostilities in Iran repeatedly in the lead-up to Election Day.

“I’m not happy with Trump,” Fitzpatrick told CNBC in October.

“I take him out of the equation,” he told The Washington Sun’s Paul Kane.

Fitzpatrick voted against the final version of the Republican's sweeping tax-cut bill in 2025 and told reporters throughout the campaign that if not for Pennsylvania’s closed-party voting system, he would have re-registered as an independent.

Christopher Nicholas, a Republican political consultant in Pennsylvania, told The Sun that Fitzpatrick has always bucked traditional party conventions, which had historically propelled Fitzpatrick to victory in Bucks County.

“He is a special guy with a special background doing a special thing,” Nicholas said. “I think him being a moderate is not a foxhole conversion. It’s something that has been true for years. In previous cycles, he’s been primaried by more conservative Republicans."

But Nicholas noted that the area is bluer than other battleground districts around the state and swung narrowly for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

“That was always one of the things that the Fitzpatricks used to do. They could appeal to the lower Bucks blue-collar folks because they were from there, while still getting the Republicans in the county to come along with them as well,” Nicholas said, adding that today’s political climate makes attracting both sides more difficult.

Still, bucking Trump would have been Fitzpatrick’s only realistic path to victory, given the profile of his district, said J. Miles Coleman, an editor at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics.

“Charitably, Trump’s approval rating is 40% nationwide,” Coleman said. “That’s one of only three congressional districts in the country that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 but sent a Republican in Congress.”

A bit more than an hour’s drive to the west, where the 10th District sprawls out from Harrisburg, Scott Perry embraced his party and campaigned alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson, a staunch ally of the president’s, in the closing days of the election cycle.

The 13-year incumbent closely aligned himself with the president, blaming media coverage for Trump’s low poll numbers and defending the administration’s war in Iran.
Election 2026-Congress-Pennsylvania (7605x5070, AR: 1.50)“All they get is bad news from the people that have the biggest megaphone that are screaming that they hate Donald Trump 24 hours a day, 365 days a year,” Perry told Newsmax in October. “A lot of great things are happening in the world.”

Perry’s alignment with the president was not a departure from his longtime political persona. A former chair of the conservative Freedom Caucus, Perry had long campaigned on lower taxes and opposition to federal overreach.

But Perry has had to run in a more competitive district since Pennsylvania redrew its congressional maps in 2018. That’s made electoral success harder for the incumbent, who beat Janelle Stelson by just 1 point in 2024.

“Even though Trump carried the district by 4 or 5 points, that district has been moving Democratic every cycle,” Coleman said.

Nicholas said it wasn’t surprising to see Perry struggle, given the circumstances. His close association with Trump didn’t help in a battleground district.

“Scott [Perry]’s district changed,” Nicholas said ahead of Election Day. “His district got less Republican. So you combine that with this being the midterm election, the turnout matrix is different, the unpopular president now is a Republican, not a Democrat, like it was two years ago.”

Still, Coleman added, Perry may have calculated that hugging Trump was important to juice up turnout among the Republican base.

Staying in lockstep with an unpopular Trump, Nicholas said, meant that Perry’s most likely path to victory was attacking Stelson for “her foibles and missteps.”

“They both won victories in 2024, back when the unpopular president was the Democrat Joe Biden. Now the unpopular incumbent president is a Republican. So that changes a lot of the kind of political culture and environment that you're in,” Nicholas said.

entries.title: Thune Expected to Run for Republican Leader Despite Heavy Midterm Losses
entries.summary: Leadership elections are scheduled Tuesday, and the South Dakota Republican still wants to lead his conference.
entries.content:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune is still expected to run for a second term atop the Republican conference despite the heavy losses incurred by his party in the midterms.

A source close to the leader confirmed the plans to The Washington Sun. Leadership elections for Senate Republicans are slated for Tuesday, Nov. 10.

The South Dakota Republican has indicated in past months that he would run to keep his leadership post, but he stopped short of making a definitive announcement. So far, no other Republican has publicly said they would challenge him.

Thune would be running for minority leader after his party saw at least six seats flip, most in ruby-red states that President Donald Trump won handily in 2024.

In a social media post, Thune signaled the Republicans’ need in the coming months and years to “stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”

“Over the last two years, Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that’s created safer streets, more money in Americans’ pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead,” Thune wrote on X. “After fighting Democrat obstruction at every turn, we prevented the largest tax hike in American history, secured our border in an unprecedented way, confirmed the president’s Cabinet at the fastest pace in two decades, and put strong conservative judges on benches across the country faster than we have since the Reagan administration.”

“I’m proud of our team and everything we’ve done for the American people, and I’m looking forward to the important work we have in front of us over the next few months. As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” Thune continued. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream.”

Thune is up for reelection in 2028. He told The Sun in an interview last week that he plans to put the “wheels in motion fairly quickly” on that front, having said separately in August that it was his “assumption” that he will seek a fifth term.

“We’ll start putting the wheels in motion fairly quickly on that,” he said about a timeline for a decision. “I’m fully confident that we can survive both primary and general elections, but it’s got to be the right thing to do. That’s always a conversation my wife and I have — kind of about where we are in life, and where we think we can make the biggest difference, and I feel like the job I have right now is a bit of a calling.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘A New Day in D.C.’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 3, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Janeese Lewis George, Robert White and more winners from Election Day in the DMV. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 10/10. Doesn't have to be a cloudless sky for a perfect score. This one's got plenty of sun, comfortable humidity and sweet highs in the 70s! Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

The day before she was elected mayor of D.C., Janeese Lewis George thought about how far she’d come since her days as a student at Rudolph Elementary, moon-eyed when then-Mayor Sharon Pratt Kelly paid her class a visit.

“I just was thinking how blessed [I am], to have seen representation growing up and to believe that I could one day be able to lead my city,” she told The Washington Sun. “That's what makes D.C. so special, and so I'm so grateful for all of the people who have led before me, and that I get to stand on their shoulders and do this work.”

Now, the work begins. Lewis George claimed an expected victory on Election Day, securing 84% of the votes counted by 9:30 p.m., marking the end of Mayor Muriel Bowser’s 12 years in office and the start of a new era in D.C. politics, The Sun’s Metro team reports.

“It’s a new day in D.C., one where we don’t make excuses or retreat,” Lewis George said in a victory speech.

What’s on her agenda? The democratic socialist campaigned on ambitious promises that drew favorable comparisons to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, such as constructing 72,000 housing units in five years and offering universal child care. She’ll face headwinds getting there. Namely, a budget deficit for 2028 that could approach $800 million, a stalled housing market and an economy hammered by federal layoffs. But Lewis George was undeterred by her detractors while casting a vote for herself Tuesday.

“I am going to be a mayor for everyone,” she said. “My goal is to make sure residents in the District of Columbia are safe, that everybody here can thrive.”

jlg_edits/2026-11-3 Midterm Election Coverage (Washington Sun)-6 copy.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)
Robert White also claimed an expected victory, winning the race to become D.C.’s nonvoting congressional delegate after a dramatic home stretch that could have seen him ruled ineligible for the position, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports.

The Democratic lawmaker, who vacated his at-large council seat Monday, became the third-ever D.C. delegate, with 87% of the votes counted by 9:30 p.m. White succeeds his former boss and mentor Eleanor Holmes Norton, who held the position for 18 terms.

“These are hard, nearly impossible shoes to fill,” White told The Sun. “But I think [voters] feel like if someone can do it, maybe I can.”

Democratic council members Matthew Frumin (Ward 3), Zachary Parker (Ward 5) and Charles Allen (Ward 6) easily won reelection, as did Aparna Raj, who will become a first-time council member and represent Ward 1. Phil Mendelson wins another term as council chair, and Oye Owolewa pulls a commanding lead in the first ranked votes of the at-large race, with At-Large council member Elissa Silverman in second place. Democratic D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb won his race, as did shadow Sen. Paul Strauss and Rep. Franklin Garcia. A full list of results can be found on the D.C. Board of Elections website.





DEEP DIVE

Foie gras is foie going, going, gone. D.C. voters passed a ballot initiative that will ban the production and sale of the delicacy, which is produced by force-feeding ducks and geese, The Sun’s Will Hofmann reports.

It’s a victory for the group of animal rights activists that have poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into the initiative’s passage, despite some prominent chefs and restaurateurs urging residents to duck it.

Some voters said it was the ballot initiative’s vivid language, describing the practice as the “force-feeding of birds to enlarge their livers,” that swayed them.

“We didn’t know a lot about it, but we didn’t like force-feeding poor ducks, so we voted for the initiative," said one Ward 3 voter.

The ban is expected to go into effect July 1. A spokesperson for Pro-Animal Future previously told The Sun the measure could deliver a blow to the entire foie gras industry — the District is the “third top consumer of foie gras,” they said.

103274 (5823x3882, AR: 1.50)



FROM THE DISTRICT

One of the day's biggest shakeups didn't involve an election. Independent At-Large council member Christina Henderson announced yesterday that she has filed paperwork to re-affiliate as a Democrat, throwing the process to replace White into flux, The Sun’s Metro team reports. Typically, D.C.’s Democratic party would find an interim replacement for the seat White vacated Monday, a process he and several other council members publicly endorsed. But only three of the council’s five at-large seats can belong to the same party — with her switch, Henderson snags the Democrats’ No. 3 slot (and sets herself up for a run at a higher council office).

D.C. Democratic Party leadership is attempting to take back the reins. Two people familiar with the party’s deliberations told The Sun that because of a D.C. code provision limiting how close to an election a voter can change their party affiliation, Henderson’s party switch did not actually go into effect on Tuesday — leaving them just enough time to nominate a candidate that afternoon. Their selection was Jamal Holtz, president of the D.C. Young Democrats. Holtz, however, is just a placeholder who will resign once the party completes its nomination process.

It’s unclear who is on solid legal ground here and what happens next.

D.C. Council member Brooke Pinto made it clear in an X post on Election Day that National Guard troops and federal agents were instructed to stay away from polling locations across the District, after D.C. leaders heard concerns from residents.

It came as several cities and counties across the country rejected the Trump administration’s election monitors from entering polling sites on Election Day, requiring the federal observers to stand 100 feet away, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports.

New plans for the massive redevelopment of East Potomac Golf Links project the cost and timeline for a new seawall and a tiered-pricing concept, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. The 55-page proposal, submitted Friday to the National Capital Planning Commission by the Interior Department, estimates the new seawall would cost $304.5 million and would take two-and-a-half to three-and-a-half years to complete.





FROM VIRGINIA

Democratic incumbents representing northern Virginian congressional districts cruised to victory yesterday. Mark Warner won a fourth term in the Senate over Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa. Reps. Don Beyer, Suhas Subramanyam and James Walkinshaw also won reelection in their districts.

Voters passed three amendments to Virginia’s constitution that were on the ballot. People with felony convictions will now automatically gain voting rights on their release from incarceration; access to abortion, contraception and fertility treatments will be protected; and same-sex marriage is enshrined in the state’s constitution.

In local races, Democratic incumbent Matt de Ferranti was reelected to the Arlington County Board. Kirsten Lockhart was voted mayor of the city of Fairfax and Erin Rayner was voted mayor of Purcellville.





FROM MARYLAND

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore easily won his reelection bid, defeating Republican challenger Dan Cox in a 2022 rematch.

The Associated Press called the race for Moore, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, minutes after the polls closed at 8 p.m.

Maryland voters approved Question 3, amending the state’s constitution to allow the Democrat-majority state assembly to redraw the congressional map ahead of 2028.

Moore sent the question to the ballot after lawmakers approved it during a special session in August. Moore said at the time that the state could not be caught “flat-footed” as President Donald Trump asked Republican-led states to redraw their congressional districts, and that passing the amendment helped ensure Maryland remain in the “national conversation.”





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For cinephiles: Film critic A.S. Hamrah at Lost City Books, Thursday.

For day drinkers: D.C. Beer Fest at Nats Park, Saturday.

For cat lovers with kids: Pages and Purrs at Politics and Prose, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

The MLB offseason kicked off Monday, and the Nationals have plenty of items on their to-do list for the next few months. Among them: Find competent relievers, land a high-upside bat and make a decision on C.J. Abrams.

But, as The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty writes, any discussion of the offseason must include the fact that professional baseball is in the early stages of a nasty labor battle that will almost certainly result in a lockout.

The playoffs have arrived for many fall sports, and The Sun’s Noah Ferguson is tracking the area’s best high school athletes. See his latest selections for All-DMV Player of the Week in football, volleyball and soccer.

entries.title: D.C. Youth Want a Seat at the (Council's) Table
entries.summary: Young members of a local nonprofit are hoping to create a new youth governing council in the District.
entries.content:
One of the toughest decisions faced by members of the Black Swan Academy during a recent tour of the Wilson Building was what to eat for lunch. Pizza was the obvious choice, but a delivery order fell through. It took about half an hour for the young advocates to settle on chicken as the backup plan.

Around a dozen members of the BSA, a local nonprofit that advocates for Black youth, visited the D.C. Council headquarters earlier this week with an ambitious goal: find a council member to sponsor legislation that would create a Youth Governing Council.

“I think it's so important for us to have a seat at the table right now, with everything that's going on and D.C. autonomy and youth autonomy being at risk,” said 17-year-old Nubia Binyam, who goes to Benjamin Banneker High School.

The new youth council would be made up of 35 members between the ages of 11 and 22, representing all eight wards. The hope is that this group would have the power to weigh in on any legislation brought before the D.C. Council. The effort would also revise the D.C. Youth Advisory Council Establishment Act of 2002, allowing members of the council to receive academic credit, community service hours or compensation up to $2,400 a year for their time.

“This would be really important because a lot of kids need jobs to support their families,” Binyam said. “They should also be able to weigh in on the government and have a seat. It shouldn't just be for people who already are provided for.”

Almost all council members were out of their offices the day of the BSA’s visit, leaving the group to speak mostly with senior staff members. With several new council members expected in January, the young organizers don’t expect their legislation to be adopted this fall.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Organizers like Binyam say they want the YGC to have a say on all legislation that impacts young people in the city, including conflict-resolution measures and other youth programs. After an initial application process and interviews, D.C. Council members would be able to appoint three representatives from their respective wards. At least three members of the youth council would be made up of young people from homes earning less than 60% of the city’s median income. The group would have advisers and a coordinator, who serves as a full-time staff member.

This is not the first time that Black Swan has tried to get a bill on the council’s radar. Members of the organization tried to introduce similar legislation last year. On Monday’s visit, organizers carried wallets stuffed with play money, a prop meant to symbolize one of the group’s core issues: affordability.

Another major issue is the city’s permanent curfew. In July, legislation created through the Youth Curfew Amendment Act of 2026 went into effect across the city. It prohibits anyone under the age of 18 from being out in public places after midnight on Fridays and Saturdays, or after 11 p.m. between Sunday and Thursday during the school year.

“You can't even walk anywhere or go anywhere without someone assuming that you're going to a teen takeover,” said 15-year-old Cymiah Best, a 10th grader at McKinley Tech High School.

A lack of third spaces for teens and “the overpolicing” of young people, especially by federal agents and the National Guard, were also prominent topics in the group’s early discussions around a council.

“As a youth, this could really impact the way we think about police because you know some people be like, ‘Police are bad,’ but it comes from somewhere,” 15-year-old Naomi Bonilla said. “It doesn't just naturally happen.”

Thursday

Opening Night at the Double Exposure Film Festival

Johns Hopkins Bloomberg Center Theater, 555 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, 6:15 p.m., pay what you can

Where’d the Van Gogh go? Art heists are a hugely popular subgenre of true crime stories, so it’s no coincidence that the Double Exposure Film Festival is opening with the U.S. premiere of “The Oligarch and the Art Dealer,” a new film about a Russian billionaire and the Swiss gallerist who stashed paintings by Klimt, Chagall, Van Gogh and more in a mysterious vault on his behalf. A Q&A with director Andreas Dalsgaard and reception follows. The documentary-focused festival runs through Sunday.

Film critic A.S. Hamrah at Lost City Books

2467 18th St. NW, 7 p.m., free

The film critic for n+1, The Baffler, The New York Review of Books and other outlets discusses his new collection, “Algorithm of the Night,” with former Washington Post pop music critic Chris Richards.

More to explore: Q Marsden’s neo-soul at Union Stage.

Friday

Punch Brothers at the Warner Theatre

513 13th St. NW, 8 p.m. $49 to $120

“Ahoy there!” Inland or not, that’s how mandolinist Chris Thile prefers to greet his audiences. The MacArthur Genius grant winner and host of the late, great public radio show “Live from Here” brings his band of bluegrassy/sea shanty/classical-ish musicians to the Warner.

Asia After Dark: Diwali Festival at the National Museum of Asian Art

1050 Independence Avenue SW, 5 to 9 p.m., free

The Smithsonian celebrates the Hindu festival of lights with an after-hours extravaganza. Food vendors and kid-focused crafts open at 5 p.m. Docent talks and tours of the museum’s collections continue throughout the evening, while music and dance performances run from 5:30 to 7:30. That’s when DJ MAIYA takes over to spin South Asian tunes, while outside, the museum is lit up in vibrant, swirling hues.

More to explore: All Hallows’ Eve Celtic concert at the Hill Center

Saturday

WNO’s “Madama Butterfly” at DAR Constitution Hall 

1776 D St. NW, 7 p.m., $60 to $250
Madama Butterfly WNO (1659x948, AR: 1.75)The Washington National Opera opens its first full non-Kennedy Center season with Puccini’s gut-wrenching classic about a geisha abandoned by an American sailor. For this immersive staging, the company built a custom thrust stage backed by projection screens and hung a giant cloud of cherry blossoms from Constitution Hall rafters.

An Evening with Kate Nash at Hamilton Live

600 14th St. NW, 8 p.m., $31 to $43

The Anglo-Irish indie singer-songwriter Kate Nash’s music was wildly popular in mid-aughts indie circles, but the economics of pop music have changed. The tour supporting her new album “Cailin,” is partly funded by her account on OnlyFans. “It’s literally funding my tour,” Nash told The Independent in 2024. “Shining a light on my ass is shining a light on the issue [of funding] in the music industry.”

More to explore: DC Beer Fest at Nats Park

Sunday

“On Stage: Portraying the Performing Arts” opens at the National Portrait Gallery

8th and G Streets NW, 11:30 a.m. to 7 p.m., free

Increased restrictions and oversight from the Trump administration have translated into fewer major exhibits opening at federal museums. Instead, we’re seeing smaller displays drawn from permanent collections. This weekend, the National Portrait Gallery opens “Portraying the Performing Arts,” featuring 20 portraits of people who became famous on American stages, from Ginger Rogers to LL Cool J.

“Wish You Were Here” closes at Studio Theatre

1501 14th St. NW, 2 p.m., $93

The sophomore effort from Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Sanaz Toossi is set in 1978 Iran, where a group of girlfriends prepares for an elaborate wedding and a revolution with a mix of giddiness and trepidation.
