entries.title: All-DMV High School Soccer Players of Week 10
entries.summary: This week’s group features a clutch goalkeeper from The Heights and a red-hot forward from Potomac School.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

Week 10 of the high school soccer season marked the first opportunity for the DMV’s best to earn postseason hardware. Here’s who stood out in a consequential stretch:

Matthew Caban, Junior, Forward, Wootton

Caban missed a chunk of the Wootton boys’ regular season after picking up an injury in early September. He returned in October and has been lights-out ever since — the junior forward has scored four goals and seven assists in Wootton’s last six matches, five of which were wins.

In the team’s region semifinal matchup against Northwood last week, his goal helped Wootton race out to a 2-0 first-half lead. After the Gladiators responded with two goals in the final 15 minutes of the second half, Caban drew a crucial penalty kick with less than three minutes left. The Patriots put it away to advance to the next round of the playoffs in a 3-2 win.

Giselle Falcon, Senior, Forward, Good Counsel

The aptly named Falcon, one of the Good Counsel girls’ senior captains, spent much of October abroad, representing Puerto Rico in the FIFA U17 World Cup in Morocco. She returned home just in time for the Falcons’ Washington Catholic Athletic Conference playoff push last week and made her mark, scoring the lone goal in a 1-0 semifinal win over St. John’s. She then scored another goal to help send Sunday’s title game against Paul VI to penalty kicks.

She scored the deciding goal in the shootout as Good Counsel earned its 15th conference title under longtime coach Jim Bruno.

“Every time she touched the ball [Sunday], the flock of defenders was amazing, how they came up on her,” Bruno said. “You have to account for her if you’re the other team, no matter what you think.”

Elias Hughes, Junior, Goalkeeper, The Heights

The Heights boys climbed back to the top of the WCAC on Sunday, earning a 1-0 victory over Gonzaga to clinch their third conference title since joining in 2019. Hughes, the team’s reliable goalkeeper, kept a clean sheet against one of the most potent offenses in the DMV.

His key saves were vital in the win, which helped The Heights avenge last year’s 1-0 loss to the Eagles in the same game. The win also capped an undefeated season for coach Colin Gleason’s team, a campaign that included victories over many of the top teams in the region.

“His distribution, his game management … his impact was enormous,” Gleason said of his keeper.

Chiara Mizzo, Senior, Forward, Potomac School

Mizzo closed out her regular season on a tear for the Potomac School girls. The senior — who leads the Panthers’ attack alongside her twin sister, Kaida — scored two goals in a 4-0 win over Holton-Arms last week.

The victory helped Potomac School clinch the regular season Independent School League title against one of the area’s top programs. The Panthers capped off their regular season with a 5-1 win over National Cathedral on Monday and now enter the playoffs on an eight-game winning streak.

Morgan Parks, Junior, Forward, Eleanor Roosevelt

Parks has been a crucial offensive piece in another dominant season for the Eleanor Roosevelt girls, who last week earned a victory over CMIT North in the Prince George’s County title game and later started their postseason quest for a state title with a 7-0 rout of Paint Branch.

Parks came out blazing hot in the latter win. She scored a hat trick in the first 13 minutes, then later added a fourth goal as the Raiders ran away with the win. The junior is now up to 14 goals and two assists on the season.

Oswaldo Reynosa, Senior, Midfield, Parkdale

The Parkdale boys won another Prince George’s County title in dominant fashion last week, handing Fairmont Heights its first loss of the season with a 6-0 victory to win the crown. Reynosa, the team’s steady senior leader, scored the opening goal in the contest as the Panthers rolled to a comfortable win.

Days later, Reynosa helped coach William Sama’s team to a 3-0 win over DuVal in the opening round of the playoffs. With Reynosa leading the charge, the Panthers once again look like bona fide Maryland 4A state title contenders.

entries.title: How Sports Candidates Fared in the Midterms
entries.summary: Mark Teixeira will be in the next Congress. Michele Tafoya will not.
entries.content:
One parallel between sports and politics is that games and elections come down to the same binary: Outside of very specific instances, including many soccer matches, you either win or lose.

So, on Tuesday night, those were the familiar stakes for a handful of candidates with a background in sports, from a former MLB All Star to a longtime sideline reporter. Here’s how they all fared in the midterm elections, which resulted in the Democrats flipping control of the Senate and House in a massive blue wave:

In House races …

  • Republican Mark Teixeira (former MLB All Star) won Texas’s 21st Congressional District, defeating Democrat Kristin Hook. 
  • Republican Jay Feely (former NFL kicker) is heading toward a loss to Democrat Amish Shah in Arizona’s 1st District. Most of the vote was in as of Wednesday morning, putting Shah on the verge of flipping the seat for Democrats. (Shah was the New York Jets’ team doctor at the same time Feely was the team’s kicker. In a twist, then, a Jet was always guaranteed to win.)
  • Democrat Colin Allred (former NFL linebacker) won Texas’s 33rd Congressional District, defeating Republican Patrick David Gillespie. 
In Senate races …

  • Republican Michele Tafoya (longtime sideline reporter, including on “Sunday Night Football” for more than a decade) lost to Democrat Peggy Flanagan for Minnesota’s open Senate seat.  
  • Democrat Josh Turek (D-Iowa, two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball) defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson for Iowa’s open Senate seat. 
In gubernatorial races …

  • Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville (former Division I football coach, most notably at Auburn) defeated Democrat Doug Jones to become Alabama’s next governor. 
There are different levels to these sports backgrounds, in that Teixeira is much more known for his baseball career than Allred is for his football days. And if you dig deep enough, many more of the midterm candidates had some connection to sports, tenuous or otherwise. Before losing his Senate seat in Ohio to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Tuesday, Republican Jon Husted (R-Ohio) played college football at Dayton. Before losing to Amy Acton in Ohio’s gubernatorial race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy took a few curious hacks in a batting cage.

But as for sports-driven name recognition, the four Republicans above — Teixeira, Tuberville, Tafoya and Feely — are in a different category than the Democrats. It’s another example of how Republicans don’t just mine sports for political talking points, but also for candidates with built-in fame.

Tafoya won’t get to see how that could have helped her in office. Neither will Feely unless something dramatically changes Wednesday. Teixeira, on the other hand, has already been angling to join the House’s powerful Financial Services Committee as a freshman, as The Washington Sun reported in October. His connections in New York, where he won a World Series with the Yankees in 2009, should help his chances, even as Republicans lose committee seats.

Asked whether Democrats might use this strategy more in future elections, multiple strategists said it could make sense in long-shot swing districts that have typically favored Republicans (and if the right candidate existed). For example, in 2025, a polling firm tested former Cardinals pitcher Adam Wainwright against Republican Ann Wagner in Missouri’s 2nd Congressional District. Wainwright quickly said he wasn’t interested. On Tuesday, Wagner instead lost her seat to Fred Wellman, an Army veteran.

“For every Mark Teixeira for the Republicans, there’s a cautionary tale like Herschel Walker in Georgia, right?” a Democratic strategist told The Sun Tuesday night, as Democrats were running up the score across the country. “It’s circumstantial, like anything, but it obviously can help to run someone who’s already known for something other than politics. You just want it to feel natural, not forced. That’s a really fine line.”

entries.title: Democrats Do the Unexpected: Capture a Majority of Governorships
entries.summary: It's the first time in nearly two decades that Democrats will occupy a majority of governors’ offices.
entries.content:
The Democratic Party captured a majority of governors’ offices for the first time in nearly two decades.

Govs. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Wes Moore of Maryland and JB Pritzker of Illinois were shoo-ins to win their reelection bids, but as affordability concerns motivated voters, other Democratic gubernatorial candidates were able to eke out victories in tight races against Republican opponents in solidly red states, shifting the balance of power nationwide.

One shocking upset came in Texas, where Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the state’s first Democratic governor since 1994.

Ann Richards, the state’s last Democratic governor, was unseated by George W. Bush, who served as the state’s governor from 1995 to 2000 and went on to become president.

Hinojosa, soon to be the state’s first Latina governor, proved to be the most formidable of Abbott’s opponents, overcoming a cash disadvantage as the incumbent sought a record fourth term in a race the Cook Political Report classified as “lean Republican.”

In a concession speech Tuesday night, Abbott said he called Hinojosa to congratulate her and said serving Texas for the past 12 years has been the “greatest honor” he’s ever had.

Democrat Amy Acton joined Hinojosa in flipping a previously Republican seat by winning over Vivek Ramaswamy in a state that voted Republican in the last three presidential elections.

The race between Acton and Ramaswamy turned personal when the Ramaswamy campaign spent $1 million on an attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother calling the Democratic candidate a “liar.” The ad, which garnered widespread condemnation from both parties, drew on Acton’s painful family history: Her mother reportedly sided with Acton’s stepfather, who was accused of sexually abusing her as a child.

Despite the backlash, Vice President JD Vance told upset Republicans to “stop whining.” Trump concurred, referring to the ad as “hitting pay dirt.”

“The healing begins today,” Acton told a crowd of supporters after she was projected to become Ohio’s first Democratic governor in 20 years and the first woman to fill the role. Acton said the results show Ohio chose “union and decency over division and hate.”

In all, 17 women — 10 Democrats and seven Republicans — are set to occupy governors’ offices across the country, a new record.

Rob Sand faced similar headwinds in Iowa, a GOP-stronghold state that also voted for Trump in the last three elections. Like Acton, Sand flipped Iowa’s governor seat to become the state’s first Democratic governor since 2006, running on a platform that eschewed partisanship.

In another historic victory, Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the first Black woman to serve as a U.S. governor after winning her race in Georgia.

Bottoms, in a victory speech Tuesday night, said she planned to govern like “Trump with a Southern tone” and predicted that she would become the president’s “favorite governor.”

David Crowley also made history in Wisconsin with a win over Republican Tom Tiffany to become the state’s first Black governor. When he takes office in January, Crowley will join four other Black governors, another new record.

“People who work together will win, not Democrats, not Republicans, but people, y’all. And I learned that people beats money and power each and every single day,” Crowley said in his victory speech, according to Wisconsin Public Radio. Crowley joined other victorious governors, including Bottoms, in bemoaning the massive amount of money thrown into this election cycle. Bottoms said no amount could ever “overcome the power of the people.”

It was not a clean sweep for Democrats, however. One outlier was Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who beat her Democratic opponent, Memphis City Council member Jerri Green, in one of the country’s tightest gubernatorial races.

Blackburn squeaked out the victory by 2 percentage points, making her Tennessee’s first female governor. In her victory speech, Blackburn said her campaign took a “grassroots approach.”

entries.title: Blue Wave Brings in Historic Firsts
entries.summary: Election night saw states elect their first Black, Latino and Native American governors, along with unprecedented wins in the Senate.
entries.content:
The midterm election brought a wave of historic firsts along with seismic shake-ups in Congress. As of next year, the U.S. will have its first Muslim U.S. senator, its first Black female governor, its first openly gay male senator, and more.

State governors’ races featured the most unprecedented wins.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was the first Black woman elected governor in United States history. Her decisive win in Georgia comes eight years after Stacey Abrams lost in a painfully tight race for the state’s governorship.

Wisconsin, Nevada and Florida elected their first Black governors. David Crowley, a Democrat from Wisconsin; Aaron Ford, a Democrat from Nevada; and Byron Donalds, a Republican from Florida, claimed victories in key races.

“Tonight, Wisconsin made history,” Crowley said. “Being your next governor is humbling in its own right. I don’t take any of this light, and I know exactly the shoulders that I stand on.”

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is currently the only sitting Black governor in the U.S.

California and Texas, both with populations that are approximately 40% Hispanic, elected their first Hispanic governors. Xavier Becerra won in California, while Gina Hinojosa delivered a shocking win over sitting Republican Governor Greg Abbott in Texas.

Other historic wins include New Mexico’s Deb Haaland, who will be the first Native American woman to serve as governor in the U.S., and Amy Acton, who is the first woman elected governor of Ohio.

“And tonight, in our nation’s 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected in the United States,” Haaland said. “Tonight isn’t only about history. It’s about our future.”

The Senate was a hotbed of firsts as well. Michigan elected the nation’s first Muslim senator in Abdul El-Sayed. Annie Andrews became the first woman to win a Senate election in South Carolina. Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota became the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate.

Chris Pappas, a Democrat from New Hampshire, is the first openly gay man to be elected to the Senate.

Some historically red states also saw transgender and nonbinary people elected to state legislatures for the first time. Alabama elected Allison Montgomery and Georgia voters elected Bentley Hudgins.

entries.title: Montana Voters Approve Limits on Corporate Political Spending
entries.summary: But the “Montana Plan” is expected to face legal challenges.
entries.content:
Voters in Montana approved a ban on political spending by corporations, nonprofits and other organizations, the Associated Press projected.

The ballot measure prohibits “artificial persons” that do business in Montana from spending money to influence local, state and federal elections. Violating the ban would result in them losing their ability to operate in the state.

The plan would not prevent individual megadonors from spending millions to influence elections, but it does stanch their ability to influence elections through nonprofits or other “dark money” groups that aren’t required to disclose their donors.

The so-called “Montana Plan” will all but certainly face legal challenges, mostly from conservative and libertarian free speech advocates who have fought similar efforts in states from Hawaii to Massachusetts.

Montana is the base of a broader effort by the nonprofit Transparent Election Initiative to regulate spending in elections. Americans across the political spectrum are frustrated with the amount of money in politics, which they believe drowns out the voices of the average voter in favor of special interests.

The amount of money in American politics has exploded since 2010, when the Supreme Court’s decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission allowed corporations and other outside groups to spend unlimited funds to influence elections. The decision also gave rise to super PACs.

OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks the flow of money in politics, estimates around $11.9 billion will be spent on federal elections this cycle.

That’s $1.7 billion more than political actors spent during the 2022 midterms — but still less than the National Retail Federation expected Americans to spend on Halloween this year, Owen Yeates, a senior attorney at the Institute for Free Speech, told The Washington Sun.

“Is it really too much to spend when we are deciding the people who are going to be governing us and setting the laws over us for the next two or four or six years?” Yeates said.

Yeates and the Institute for Free Speech filed a lawsuit in Hawaii earlier this year challenging a ban, signed into law in May by Democratic Gov. Josh Green, on corporate, nonprofit and union spending to influence state elections.

In September, the American Civil Liberties Union filed an amicus brief opposing the ban. The civil rights organization described the ban as “premised on an untenable theory of plenary government power over the speech rights of civil society organizations.”

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce also filed a lawsuit in September challenging the Hawaii ban, arguing it infringes upon the First Amendment right of Americans to band together to make their voices heard through associations or organizations.

“It should be left to us to be able to decide who we want to listen to, and not have the government tell us who we can hear,” Yeates told The Sun.

entries.title: Voters Back Abortion Rights and Reject Trump’s Redistricting in State Ballot Measures
entries.summary: Other measures put the president’s priorities to the test by gauging support for his attempts to limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter ID requirements.
entries.content:
By David A. Lieb

Abortion-rights advocates notched victories in several states Tuesday, and voters delivered a double dose of disapproval to President Donald Trump’s redistricting efforts as they decided 145 ballot questions in more than three dozen states.

The ballot measures provided a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election in which Democrats took control of Congress and gained power in state legislatures and gubernatorial offices.

Some measures put Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to redraw congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.

Abortion rights prevail in three states

Voters defeated a proposed amendment to Missouri’s constitution that would have reimposed restrictions on most abortions. The vote Tuesday essentially reaffirmed voters' decision from two years ago, when they became the first in the nation to undo an existing abortion ban by approving an abortion-rights amendment.

The Republican-led Legislature then referred a new, less restrictive version of an abortion ban to this year’s ballot. The measure would have allowed abortions only for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, or in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. It also would have amended the constitution to prohibit certain medical procedures for transgender minors.

Abortion-rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, heavily outspent abortion foes in a successful campaign to defeat the Missouri ballot measure.

In Virginia, a voter-approved measure creates a “ fundamental right to reproductive freedom ” in the state constitution, ensuring that abortions can occur during the first two trimesters of pregnancy. The amendment also creates a right to contraception and fertility care, among other things.

An amendment approved in Nevada creates a fundamental right to abortion until fetal viability, which is generally considered after 21 weeks of pregnancy. The amendment won initial voter approval in 2024 but needed a second vote this year to add it to the constitution.

Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a nationwide right to abortion in 2022, voters in more than one-fifth of the states have passed ballot measures protecting abortion rights.

But voters in Republican-leaning Idaho on Tuesday defeated a ballot measure that would have created abortion rights in state law. Current Idaho law bans abortions unless necessary to save the life of a pregnant woman, or during the first trimester of pregnancy in cases where rape or incest has been reported to law enforcement.

Abortion-rights measures failed two years ago in Florida and South Dakota.

Trump redistricting efforts rejected by voters

Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.

In Missouri, Republican lawmakers last year adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat in the Kansas City area. Opponents then gathered petition signatures to put the map to a public vote.

The new districts were used in the August primary. But courts subsequently ruled they could not be used again unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. Voters put an end to the new map by rejecting the redistricting legislation on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, voters in Democratic-led Maryland approved a constitutional amendment that could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, had urged a “yes” vote as a way to “stop Trump.”

Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.

Florida voters approve major property tax break

An amendment passed Tuesday could wipe away a significant amount of taxes for Florida homeowners — and leave local governments scrambling for revenue.

The Florida amendment was one of the nation’s most notable property tax proposals in a year when numerous politicians proposed ways to provide tax relief to residents burdened by high costs.

Florida currently exempts the first $50,000 of the value of a person’s permanent residence from many property taxes. That exemption will triple next year for non-school taxes and rise to $250,000 in 2028.

The measure was referred to the ballot during a special legislative session called by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Some local officials warn it could lead to cuts to police and fire departments, public libraries and parks.

Transgender restrictions pass in some states

Nebraska voters approved an amendment to add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution. And in Arizona, voters passed a measure that extends public school sports restrictions to private schools.

Voters in Colorado and Washington also were considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.

Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. In the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington, the measures were placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives. A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors.

California and Colorado reject new voter ID mandate

Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.

Opponents in California successfully campaigned against the amendment by linking it to Trump. The defeated California measure would have required a government-issued ID to vote in person or the last four digits of that identification number to vote by mail. The vast majority of California’s ballots are cast by mail.

Colorado voters also defeated a measure that would have required people voting by mail to include the last four digits of a government-issued identification number.

In Ohio and North Carolina, Republican-led legislatures referred measures to the ballot enhancing existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution. The measures passed in both states. A voter ID amendment also passed in Nevada.

Voters say ‘no’ to higher thresholds for ballot measures

North Dakota and South Dakota voters defeated ballot measures that would have made it harder to amend the state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. And Utah voters defeated a measure that would have required a 60% threshold to pass citizen initiatives that raise taxes.

Meanwhile, Missouri voters passed an amendment that would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.

Citizen voting measures keep racking up wins

Voters in Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved constitutional amendments reinforcing current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens. In Alaska, voters approved a citizen voting ballot question as state law.

Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.

Prior to this election, at least 15 states already had adopted similar measures over the past decade, including all eight states where they appeared on the ballot in 2024 and in Texas last year.

Arizona measure limits traffic cameras

Voters in Arizona passed a ballot measure limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.

Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.

The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.

About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

entries.title: The Washington Sun: Bluenami
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What comes after the blue wave — what Republicans are saying, what Democrats are saying, what the president is saying. Plus: A deep dive into how it happened. 

THE LATEST

A “massacre,” a “Watergate-level loss,” a “total ass-kicking from coast to coast.” Whatever you want to call it, Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered a historic, cataclysmic defeat in Tuesday’s midterms, losing at least 25 seats in the House, seven in the Senate, and their majorities in both.

The Sun’s Elena Schneider, Alex Roarty and Reese Gorman interviewed more than 50 lawmakers, candidates, senior strategists and consultants from both parties to deliver the definitive story on how the Republican coalition unraveled.

It starts with a meeting in early 2025, where Sen. Tim Scott, as the newly elected head of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said his priority was his relationship with Trump — a sentiment shared by many of his colleagues. It ends with last night’s historic drubbing.

What comes next?


Republicans: Finger-pointing. “President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves,” a White House official told The Washington Sun. Jasmine Wright, Ben T.N. Mause and Ayah Ali-Ahmad have the story of last night’s grumbling.

“The rallies didn’t matter,” said one Republican operative in Georgia of Trump’s midterm tour. “It was all baked. People are fucking pissed and they blame him, and they have good reason.”

Senate Republican leader John Thune plans to run to remain leader of the conference despite the brutal night, The Sun’s Al Weaver reports.

In the House, it’s hard to see how Speaker Mike Johnson stays the top Republican. Last night, he touted himself as the “the largest fundraiser in the history of the Republican Party, other than President Trump." But just two weeks ago, Johnson said it was “hilarious” for Democrats to think they could win 230 House seats. “I want you to record that I am laughing out loud about that,” he told Punchbowl News. “That is nonsense.”

To underscore the scale of Republican losses: Rep. Richard Hudson, the man in charge of the House GOP’s campaign apparatus, appeared on track to lose his seat.

Democrats: Victory laps and promises to keep. “Wow! Wow! Wow!” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said last night as he spoke to reporters.

“This is a change election, and we understand, as House Democrats, that we need to deliver dramatic change,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, said at his own press conference.

Follow The Sun’s live blog for news and analysis on the aftermath.

The White House: “Lawyer up,” Rep. Robert Garcia, the expected next chair of the House Oversight Committee, posted on X. We have reported extensively on Democratic plans to subpoena and investigate Trump officials when they take back control of the gavels on Capitol Hill. It will be a different world for an administration used to a (mostly) rubber-stamp Congress.

“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” Trump told The New York Times. “We’ll probably work something out.”

Redistricting: Will this keep going? “If they stop, we stop!” an operative familiar with Democrats’ redistricting strategy told The Sun’s Manuela Silva as the Republicans’ newly drawn lines failed to stop the Democratic wave.

The country: New faces, new competitive places. History was made across the country, with the election of the first Black woman governor from either party (Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia) and the first Black Republican governor (Byron Donalds in Florida). The first Muslim senator was elected: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Democrats won statewide races in places largely foreign to the national party like Texas and Kansas. The political map has changed.

More: Democrats Blowout Republicans in Historic Midterm, Now Face Pressure to Deliver • House Democrats reach more than 100 female members  • Amid shocking GOP losses, Trump’s Iran war looms large • One Pennsylvania Republican hugged Trump, another shunned him. They both lost • Senate Democrats cross into gloating territory

  • Trump touted his Reflecting Pool success. But new problems are visible. By Maura Judkis and Meg Kelly for The Washington Post

entries.title: Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom Says He’s ‘Confident’ He Will Win
entries.summary: The margin is still extremely tight, and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also expressed confidence in her result.
entries.content:
Scott Colom said Wednesday morning that he is “confident” he is on track to becoming the first Black senator from Mississippi in well over a century, with the race extremely tight and votes still being counted.

“I am very happy with where we stand. I'm confident. I'm confident once the process lays out where we are, where the ballots are, we're gonna win,” Colom said at a press conference, surrounded by supporters.

Colom leads Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 65votes out of more than 940,000 counted by Wednesday afternoon, with about 4% of the vote outstanding, according to The Associated Press. It might take days if not weeks to determine the outcome of the race.

Hyde-Smith also suggested Tuesday she had won the election, to which Colom responded: “Bless her heart.”

The state does not have a recount mechanism in place, making it harder for a losing candidate to challenge the results. The only path in such a case would be “to challenge decisions to exclude or to include certain ballots in the tabulation under state or federal law,” according to Election Law Blog.

On top of that, a number of voters in Mississippi voted through an affidavit ballot because they did not have an ID, giving them until next Tuesday to address any issues if they arise. Mississippi also allows mail-in ballots to arrive and be counted five business days after polls have closed if the ballots were postmarked by Election Day — a law the Supreme Court upheld in June, against Republicans’ effort to eliminate it.

Colom said at the press conference that his campaign had been preparing for this moment for months and that hundreds of volunteers and local lawyers would be in “each county” to “protect the integrity of this election.”

“There are no runoffs,” Colom said as he urged voters to seek help if they need to address their affidavit ballots. “I want to make sure people know we're going to protect the process. We got lawyers who are ready to make sure the law is followed.”

Top Democrats are sending officials from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to Mississippi, sources told The Washington Sun.

They’ll be on the ground, along with the Elias Law Group, leading the party’s efforts to ensure all votes are counted, the sources said.

Democrats are trying to pad the Senate majority they’ve already secured. The party has flipped Republican seats in Texas, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa.

Colom and Hyde-Smith go way back. In 2021, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to become a federal judge, but his nomination was ultimately blocked by Hyde-Smith in 2023. 

“I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a U.S. senator,” Hyde-Smith said Tuesday night.

entries.title: Kemp Rejects Calls to Hold Special Redistricting Session
entries.summary: “The voters of our state have spoken,” Kemp said.
entries.content:
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced Wednesday that he would not call a special legislative session to redraw the state's congressional maps before Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms assumes office in January.

Kemp, a Republican who has clashed with President Donald Trump in recent years, tried to push for the state to redraw its congressional map earlier this year. The effort was ultimately rejected by the state legislature, with lawmakers citing pending legal cases against Republican redistricting pushes in other states.

Party leaders, however, did not rule out revisiting the issue later in the year, according to The Associated Press.

“I will not be calling a special session of the Georgia General Assembly in order to curtail executive branch powers or debate redistricting changes,” Kemp said in a statement shared with The Washington Sun Wednesday. He added that there are “budgetary issues that may need to be addressed before” Bottoms takes office.

Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) described Kemp’s decision as a “wise choice” in an interview with Politico on Wednesday.

Even without redrawing the maps, Georgia Republicans held an expected advantage heading into Election Day — one that failed to materialize amid a once-in-a-generation blue wave that knocked out previously safe-seat Republicans from coast to coast.

It remains unclear if Kemp spoke with state lawmakers before making his Wednesday announcement. Georgia’s Republican House majority leader, Chuck Efstration, and Senate Majority Leader Jason Anavitarte did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bottoms’ win over billionaire businessman Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor’s race upended more than two decades of Republican control of the governorship in Georgia.

Kemp congratulated Bottoms, as well as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Georgia), on a “hard-fought win” in a separate statement posted on X, where he appeared to call on Republicans to turn back to more traditional conservative values.

“Republicans now have the opportunity, and responsibility, to heed the will of voters and learn from last night’s results,” Kemp wrote. “I firmly believe the conservative principles of our party lead to greater freedom, security, and prosperity for all Americans—and it’s time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come.”

Kemp has broken with Trump in the past. Most notably, Kemp and other state leaders faced Trump’s fury when they refused to help overturn the results of the 2020 election after Trump claimed without evidence that widespread voter fraud had helped former President Joe Biden capture the state.

entries.title: Vance Says the Iran War and Inflation Cost Republicans the Midterms
entries.summary: A potential 2028 contender, Trump’s No. 2 also said voters want Republicans to “Put America First” and change the country’s relationship with Israel.
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance said the reason Republicans lost Tuesday night's midterm was “obvious to almost everyone.”

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X.

A potential 2028 presidential candidate, Vance said turnout was good, but many voters shifted to Democratic candidates — costing Republicans control of both congressional chambers.

Vance said a pollster asked those voters what would bring them back to the Republican Party. The pollster told him there were four key factors: ending the Iran war, focusing on cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing the country’s relationship to Israel

The vice president said he felt “negative” going into Tuesday's election and was shocked when the pollster told him they would “lose the general ballot by 13 points.” By Tuesday night, Democrats flipped seats in historic deeply red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Vance closed the lengthy social media post by apologizing for not heeding the warning that voters were worried about the war and affordability, but urging them to take their anger to the next election.

“To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so,” Vance said. “Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview.”

entries.title: The 2028 GOP Race Is On
entries.summary: Tuesday’s brutal midterm losses sent Vice President JD Vance’s stock sinking, while the Ron DeSantis chatter started to heat up.
entries.content:
Republicans’ historic wipeout in the 2026 midterm elections is already having major ramifications for the party’s 2028 presidential race.

Republican lawmakers and commentators are downgrading the odds that Vice President JD Vance will win the party’s presidential nomination because of his role defending President Donald Trump and his administration’s policies, which led to Democrats sweeping control of the House and Senate in Tuesday’s elections. Vance was widely seen as a frontrunner for the nomination before Tuesday.

"There's one winner tonight on the Republican side, and that's Marco Rubio,” Fox News host and former Republican Rep. Trey Gowdy said of Trump’s secretary of state during an appearance on the network Wednesday morning.

He noted that Trump won't be on the ballot again, but that "for JD Vance, good luck."

Vance immediately gave his take about what happened in a long post on X Wednesday morning as he started to distance himself from the president’s policies.

“The main problem” on Tuesday night wasn’t turnout, he wrote. “The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.”

He wrote that the reason for the loss was “obvious to almost everyone” — the war in Iran, high cost of living, deemphasizing “America First” and the U.S. relationship with Israel.

“Our voters showed up,” he wrote. “And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats.”

But even as he starts to create separation from Trump now, Vance is tethered to the administration and its politics, including the war in Iran.

Indiana Rep. Marlin Stutzman wasted no time endorsing Rubio for president.

“Now that we lost majorities, we can’t push policy, so we will have to do better at communicating,” Stutzman told Fox News early Wednesday.

Rubio, who ran for president in 2016, said in September he has no current plans to run for president again.

“I don't know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time. I'm not a candidate for anything right now. And I'm 100 percent focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs,” he said, referring to his dual roles as secretary of state and national security adviser.

The former Florida senator joined Trump on the campaign trail in the weeks leading up to the election, putting a spotlight on his administration’s foreign policy achievements, including pressure campaigns regarding Venezuela and Cuba. He was also an early cheerleader for going to war in Iran, which could complicate a future presidential run.

Another potential 2028 presidential contender getting buzz in the wake of Tuesday’s results is Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who had warned about the lack of enthusiasm among Republican voters ahead of the midterms. Florida was one of the few states that pulled out Republican statewide wins, with Rep. Byron Donalds winning his bid for governor and Sen. Ashley Moody winning a closer than expected race.

“DeSantis just became the front runner for 2028 !!!!!!” wrote former Ohio Rep. Jim Renacci in a post on social media.

DeSantis was a bitter Trump primary rival in 2024 who later mended fences with the president. He’s popular with the MAGA base, but doesn’t have the baggage of Trump’s unpopular policies like Vance would — including the war in Iran, and the high cost of gas and other consumer goods — which could give him a leg up in a post-Trump presidential primary.

On Wednesday he already started to argue that his governing record in Florida puts him above the rest of the party.

“To call it a wave would not be politically accurate. It was more like a meteor strike,” DeSantis said in a press conference addressing Republicans’ disappointing midterm election results.

DeSantis positioned himself as the leader of the only state to come out of Tuesday night’s bloodbath relatively unscathed. He blamed current Republicans for losing the Senate, and predicted that conservatives would not have decisive control of Congress potentially for a decade. He credited Florida’s Republican wins on a strategic choice to include a property elimination tax initiative on the ballot, saying he “was the chief person to do that.”

Other candidates whose fortunes could rise for 2028 include prominent Trump critics such as former U.N. Ambassador and South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.

Haley argued during an interview on NBC News Tuesday that Republicans need to go back to their roots and embrace conservative policies.

“Economic freedom. Lower taxes. Smaller government … those are things we win on. When Americans feel unheard of, we lose. Republicans have not been following that playbook, especially fiscal responsibility,” Haley said.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz has been eyeing a run but may also face headwinds should he throw his hat into the ring. Now that Texas will have a Democratic governor next year in Gina Hinojosa, she would get to appoint someone to the U.S. Senate if Cruz is elected president or vice president. That could add to the Democratic majority in 2029, giving Republicans less reason to nominate Cruz.

Even as many immediately started looking ahead to 2028, Republican lawmakers and officials throughout the country were still trying to wrap their heads around the recriminations of Tuesday night.

“Americans don’t like chaos, narcissism, tariffs, corruption, Putin, rudeness to our allies, arrogance & indecency,” Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon posted on X. “The GOP should embrace our roots: free markets, economic freedom, peace through strength, federalism, law and order, low taxes, pro-life… and we should act like leaders of the free world.”

entries.title: Everything You Need to Know From Election Day in the DMV
entries.summary: If you’re just catching up: D.C. has a new mayor, Maryland approved redistricting and Virginia flipped a House seat.
entries.content:
Some of the more contentious national races had yet to be called the morning after the midterm elections, but local voters have a pretty clear idea of how candidates and initiatives in the D.C. area fared. Here’s a recap of the most pivotal races in the DMV:

D.C.


Congressional delegate: Former At-Large D.C. Council member Robert White won 87% of the votes counted to become D.C.’s nonvoting delegate to congress. He’s the third person to hold the role. White stepped down from his seat on the D.C. Council on Monday after turmoil over a 1970 law that mandates any potential delegate cannot occupy a paid political position on the day they are elected.

Foie Gras: Voters passed an initiative to ban the production and sale of foie gras, a French delicacy produced by force-feeding ducks and geese, with 73% of voters backing the measure. The ban is expected to go into effect next July. After that, foie gras lovers will have to get their fix in Maryland and Virginia, where the dish remains legal.

Mayor: Janeese Lewis George, a democratic socialist, cruised to an expected victory in the D.C. mayoral race, capturing 84% of the votes counted, according to unofficial results from the D.C. Board of Elections. She’ll be the first new mayor in 12 years, after Muriel Bowser decided not to seek reelection.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Maryland 


Governor: Gov. Wes Moore, the Democratic incumbent, won his second term, sailing to a smooth victory with 63% of votes, according to the Maryland State Board of Elections. Moore claimed victory in a rematch against Republican Dan Cox, whom he faced in the 2022 election. The governor has been frequently discussed as a potential presidential candidate in 2028. Moore has denied interest in higher office but fueled speculation as he traveled across the country to campaign for other Democrats.

Montgomery County: Democrat Will Jawando carried 78% of the vote to become the county executive of Maryland’s most populous county. Jawando, who currently serves on the county council, will be the first new county executive since 2018, succeeding Democrat Marc Elrich, who is term-limited.

Redistricting: Voters cleared the way for Maryland lawmakers to redraw the state’s congressional map, passing a constitutional amendment that changes a section of the state’s governing document that was used by a judge to throw out the last attempt at redrawing districts. The amendment, which garnered 60% of initial votes, clarifies that existing rules about boundaries only apply to state legislative districts, not congressional districts.

Virginia 

U.S. Representatives: Virginia flipped one U.S. House seat Democratic with Elaine Luria winning 53% of the vote Tuesday night in the state’s 2nd Congressional District race.

As of Wednesday morning, races for the 5th and 1st District have yet to be called by the Associated Press, with less than a 10,000 vote margin in each race. Democrat Shannon Taylor has a slight lead in the 1st District, while Republican John McGuire III leads in the 5th District.

U.S. Senate: In one of the first races called on Tuesday night, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner took a quick win in his reelection bid, with 61% of the vote. The victory sends him into his fourth term representing the commonwealth.

Voting rights: People who have completed felony sentences will automatically have their voting rights restored when their incarceration ends, after voters passed a constitutional amendment Tuesday, with 56% of the vote, according to the Virginia Department of Elections. Currently, people with felony convictions who spent time in prison or jail have to petition the governor to restore their voting rights.

entries.title: How James Talarico Turned Texas Into a 2028 Battleground
entries.summary: The Democrat's stunning win was the product of an unlikely coalition, a disciplined campaign and a toxic political environment for Republicans. It may now serve as a road map for what comes next.
entries.content:
AUSTIN, Texas — Just three weeks before Election Day, James Talarico's allies received internal polling showing him leading his Texas Senate race by 7 points. For the first time, they began to believe he might actually win, according to a person close to the campaign who shared the previously unreported numbers.

But even Talarico hadn't anticipated a victory so early Tuesday night, a person close to him said.

Talarico's stunning defeat of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, President Donald Trump's pick for the Senate seat, sent shock waves through Texas and the rest of the country. Even on an astounding night for Democrats nationwide, what happened here stands in its own stratosphere. Democrats have spent years trying to identify fissures in Republicans’ decades-long stranglehold on Texas, praying that changing state demographics could open up a new and lasting path to power. It didn’t work in 2014, when Wendy Davis’ much-hyped campaign for governor fell flat against Greg Abbott. It didn’t happen in 2018 either, when great hopes for Beto O’Rourke went bust against Ted Cruz.

But on Tuesday night, Abbott fell alongside Paxton. In the end, it wasn't even close. With nearly 90% of the votes tallied, Talarico beat Paxton by nearly 10 points.

Democrats have finally proven they can win Texas — a state with 40 votes in the Electoral College. The ripple effects over just the next two years could be dramatic.

“Texas is going to be ground zero when it comes to the Democrat and Republican parties fighting for the 40 electoral votes,” Julián Castro, the former mayor of San Antonio and a 2020 presidential candidate, told The Washington Sun. “A Democratic candidate could win in 2028. And if a Democrat takes the 40 electoral votes in Texas in the general election in 2028, it’s game over.”

What Talarico did to give Democrats their breakthrough here could serve as a guide for his party’s future.

His allies say the win didn’t happen overnight. It was the culmination of more than a year of work, a message rooted in his Christian faith and economic populism, a shift toward the political center and a fundraising operation that helped make him competitive in one of the most expensive political battlegrounds in the country.

“James is a unique, fresh voice,” said Garry Jones, the director of the pro-Talarico Lone Star Rising PAC. “He's young. He's got a very different message than your average Democrat.”

His unlikely path to becoming senator-elect began with an appearance on Joe Rogan's podcast, back when a Senate bid was still just a rumor. Then came a bruising, personal primary battle against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, which ended with Talarico getting pushed over the top by a swell of Latino voters.

On Tuesday, Talarico was able to peel off enough Republican voters and take advantage of a Latino surge to pull off a victory in a state that some of the most seasoned Democratic strategists had doubted their party could flip this cycle.

It’s difficult to understate the impact Talarico’s win will have in Texas politics going forward, Kendall Scudder, the Texas Democratic Party chair, told The Washington Sun in an interview.

“Show me another state where they're having to accomplish what we're accomplishing while also competing against $350 million,” he said, referring in part to the millions of dollars Elon Musk poured into the race to support Paxton. “The richest man in the world is dumping coppers into dragging us down, and it's not moving the needle at all because of how hard we're working, because of the infrastructure that we built.”

Texas Democrats had a historic night Tuesday beyond Talarico’s win. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa beat Abbott in a massive upset, and Democrats flipped House seats Republicans had been confident about winning, including the state’s 15th and 34th Congressional Districts.

The top three positions in Texas state government are now going to be held by Democrats. Vikki Goodwin beat incumbent Dan Patrick for lieutenant governor, and Jon Rosenthal beat Bo French for Texas railroad commissioner.

For Talarico, the challenge was forming a coalition of voters that could succeed where previous Democratic candidates had fallen short.

“James, after the primary, had to deal with this issue of Black voters, and his team … appears to have figured it out and created a lot of goodwill in the Black community,” Scudder said. “He has done an incredible job in the primary and in the general in exciting Hispanic voters, particularly in the border where Democrats have lost voters. And he has kept progressives on his side without moving too far to the left.”

But it was his inroads with disillusioned Republican voters, his allies said, that pushed him across the finish line, and it provides the clearest road map to Democrats for how to keep Texas in their column.

“We knew there was doubt in voters' minds who typically would default to Republican, and that James had unique ability to [reach out to them],” Jones said. “Not just because of his campaign style and his approach this year — and I think unique ability to connect with a wide swath of voters — but also Ken Paxton's, like, extraordinarily high negatives.”

Paxton and his allies were quiet Tuesday night. He didn’t call Talarico to concede, a person familiar with Paxton told The Sun.

“For a Democrat to win in Texas is a Herculean effort, not just because of the size and not just because of the cost,” Scudder said. “You have to build unique coalitions to even get close to your win number, which is expensive and politically taxing.”

Luke Warford, the founding partner of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund, a group in Texas that is trying to help build more Democratic infrastructure, summed up Talarico’s success as both a response to the political environment and the campaign’s hard work.

“Paxton is so bad, and Trump is so bad, and James is such a good candidate, but I just really think we shouldn't skip over like how unlikely this was a year ago,” he said. “Hundreds of people on his team and across maybe thousands of people, if you include volunteers and everything, so many people did so much work to make this happen. We shouldn't skip over that.”

One thing is clear: The attention on Texas won’t ease up anytime soon.

“If we don't have Texas or North Carolina in the Democratic column, you won't have a Democratic president anymore,” Scudder said. “We're going to be really grateful, I think, the Texas Democrats put in the infrastructure now instead of waking up the day of and deciding we needed to scramble to do it.”
entries.author: Daniella Diaz

entries.title: Musk, Crypto and Data Centers Are Among the Midterm’s Biggest Money Losers
entries.summary: They spent big in the midterms. It didn’t pay off in key races.
entries.content:
Republicans weren’t the only losers in last night’s general election.

Elon Musk, the cryptocurrency industry and data centers also got walloped, burning through hundreds of millions of dollars backing losing candidates and now must contend with powerful Democratic opponents ushered in by a “bluenami.”

Musk, the trillionaire ally of President Donald Trump who poured over $445 million into the midterms, is widely expected to be a top target for Democrats.
Elon Musk DOGE AP-25120619379198 (2290x1527, AR: 1.50)Musk’s millions overwhelmingly went into Texas’ U.S. Senate race, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk posted on X early Wednesday with a shrug emoji.

The cryptocurrency industry also suffered setbacks.

The industry-aligned super PAC Fairshake, funded primarily by industry leaders Ripple, Andreessen Horowitz and Coinbase, spent over $10 million opposing Juliana Stratton, the Democratic Senate nominee in Illinois who easily won her seat.

And Sherrod Brown, the former senator from Ohio who lost in 2024 after Fairshake spent millions to back now-Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, won his way back into the Senate last night.

Moreno has been a leading advocate on Capitol Hill for the cryptocurrency industry. At a campaign event last month, Brown he said the industry was spending against him again this election cycle because “they know I’m gonna take ‘em on.”

Several candidates backed by Fairshake and its affiliates did win Tuesday, including Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Nebraska) — who managed to fend off an independent challenger — and Sens.-elect Barry Moore in Alabama and Andy Barr in Kentucky.

Geoff Vetter, a Fairshake spokesperson, highlighted the Nebraska victory in a statement to The Washington Sun — and predicted more success to come.

“Fairshake played a meaningful role in winning competitive races across the country in 2026 and we will do it again in 2028,” Vetter wrote. “Newly elected and current members will have a choice: protect consumers and American jobs or fight progress. We will be watching and ’28 is a new map.”

The data center industry also spent heavily in the months leading up to the general election.

It didn’t go well.

Building the Future, a new pro-data industry super PAC that has not yet disclosed its donors, spent over $2.5 million on media and text messages in support of Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina), who lost in a stunning upset to Democrat Annie Andrews.
Meta Data Center (5259x2959, AR: 1.78)In September, Andrews called for a two-year moratorium on new data center projects in South Carolina. While she won’t have a vote on state policy and the federal government is unlikely to adopt a nationwide moratorium, it’s emblematic of a broader anti-data center shift.

Anti-data center forces won 38 of 39 ballot measures in states across the country, from California to Maine, according to an analysis by Redbud Consulting. Eight results are outstanding.

“They basically burned their cash,” a Democratic lobbyist granted anonymity to discuss issues that could impact clients in the data center and crypto industries told The Sun.

“If you run on something and you have hundreds of millions of dollars worth of ads run against you, and that doesn't stop you, you’re going to keep on moving and probably keep on moving more aggressively,” they said. “I think for Democrats, that’s going to be one of their focuses, and those industries are going to be in the bull’s-eye.”

While Trump still holds veto power over federal legislation, there’s plenty Democrats can do to make life difficult for these and other industries — and keep K Street busy helping clients navigate anticipated congressional investigations and oversight hearings.

“Businesses are about to find themselves dangerously sandwiched between a still powerful but unforgiving Executive Branch with whom they must work, and a righteously indignant and electorally emboldened Congress determined to find and expose corruption, which they perceive everywhere,” Bruce Mehlman, founder of bipartisan lobbying firm Mehlman Consulting, told The Washington Sun on Wednesday morning.

entries.title: What Midterms? Trump's Focusing on His Ballroom.
entries.summary: The president focuses his first public appearance after Republicans’ sweeping midterm losses on the ongoing construction at the White House.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump's first public appearance since Democrats swept the midterms was a beam signing inside the unfinished White House ballroom, where he spoke for more than 20 minutes about its yet-to-be-installed Corinthian columns, bulletproof glass and marble floor.

He did not raise the election once, though he did field reporter questions on it afterward.

"I'm at a loss," one administration official told The Washington Sun of the appearance.

Trump told the more than 500 workers gathered at the site that construction is ahead of schedule, under budget and will be "the safest place in Washington," referring to the aspects of the project he’s argued are crucial for national security.

He pointed toward the ceiling and noted they were over 50 feet high. The roof, he said, could hold more than 100 drones and the marble came from a vein the quarry owner didn't want to sell, but relented because "he liked me."

Trump has frequently retreated to the comfort of a construction project this year, as his approval rating cratered to historic lows amid concerns about high costs from the Iran war and government corruption.

On Monday, while Republican candidates made their final pitches to voters, the president visited the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial and devoted much of his speech to discussing the renovation. But at least one former administration official indicated they weren’t surprised to see Trump return to the construction site on Wednesday.

“The ballroom is his emotional support animal,” the former Trump official said.

Trump seemed to acknowledge as much during his presentation, when he alluded to some of the criticism that too much of his focus ahead of the midterms had been centered on the ballroom and other renovation projects.

"It was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign about, ‘Why does Trump spend time on the White House?’ Well, first of all, it's very little time. Second of all, I like it. It's good for me," he said. "I love construction."

"It's free," Trump said. "Some great patriots have devoted a lot of money, given a lot of money to get it built, and so we didn't use taxpayers' money to build this ballroom."

Internal documents reported by The Washington Post earlier this year put roughly $307 million drawn from taxpayer-funded sources, with the total construction cost at about $600 million.

Although Trump’s presentation didn’t mention Tuesday’s midterm catastrophe, he didn’t avoid questions about it afterward. As workers placed the final beam, he reiterated his belief that the outcome would’ve been better had he been on the ballot — “We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said — and that the cost of the Iran war had a significant impact on the election results.

“It’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term,” Trump said. “But at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again. Because, long term, it’s the only answer.”

Trump was up late on election night, giving phone interviews to reporters from The New York Times and the Wall Street Journal and also calling into shows on Fox News and Politico.

Trump wasn’t heard from publicly again until midday Wednesday, when he posted on Truth Social that the stock market “hit another Record High” and images of the New York Post’s metro edition praising his foreign policy.

entries.title: Democratic Wave Short-circuits an Election Stress Test
entries.summary: President Donald Trump said he was willing to accept the results, which Democrats called “Too big to rig.”
entries.content:
Democrats' historic election victories wiped away months of concerns that the Trump administration could bring legal challenges in close elections that could’ve stretched control of Congress into a gut-wrenching courtroom grind.

There will be an aftermath. The Justice Department has started a criminal probe over alleged ballot-stacking in Alaska's Senate race that ensnared Marc Elias, a key Democratic party lawyer. Subpoenas have gone out for election workers in California, where the Trump administration is fighting over counting of ballots they suspect are from noncitizens.

But with control of Congress all but determined Wednesday morning, the threat of widespread litigation faded outside the typical partisan clashes in close races. Some Democrats summed it up in a catchphrase: “Too big to rig.”

Even the president, who had spent months grooming his base to doubt Democratic wins, appeared conciliatory on Tuesday night, telling The New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the election results.

At the same time, he posted a photo of the traditional red MAGA hat with “VETO” written on it, calling back to his earlier threats that he would veto whatever Democrats bring to his desk if they gained congressional power.

Election officials across the country had planned for aggressive litigation and worst-case incursions by the federal government on Election Day. That work required significant investments from many of the nation’s 10,000 election jurisdictions. Some officials and advocates even raised the possibility of federal agents seizing ballots after voting or refusing to seat Democratic winners.

None of those fears materialized. Neither did concerns of immigration agents appearing at the polls or a presidential declaration of an emergency to justify intervening in voting.

And there was vanishingly small amounts of election night chaos, nowhere near the calculated or system attacks that had officials and advocates anxious. Weather events hit polling locations in Florida, Utah and Colorado; technology glitches affected some polls in states including New York, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s deployment of an unprecedented 1,000 DOJ election monitors across the country appeared to go smoothly aside from isolated dust-ups in two states. Election officials in Michigan and New Mexico said monitors in two locations asked unusual questions but both situations were quickly deescalated.

The Trump administration had spent months laying the groundwork for an array of potential legal challenges, with the nation’s top law enforcement and national security officials promoting unsubstantiated claims of noncitizen voting and security vulnerabilities.

By the close of polls on Tuesday night, many of the officials who had most loudly amplified the administration’s noncitizen voting claims had gone silent on social media. Court dockets were largely quiet. The federal courts had rejected efforts to have California set aside ballots from suspected nonvoters.

Deirdre Schifeling, chief political and advocacy officer for the American Civil Liberties Union, said almost every losing candidate has conceded publicly.

“So I think we're in a better spot in terms of actually having democracy upheld, and having peaceful transition of power, in the way that our Constitution expects and our country is used to, and that voters expect,” Schifeling said.

Still, the DOJ is pursuing the handful of cases it has left, however legally questionable they are.

A longshot DOJ lawsuit seeking to preemptively contest results in the Alaska Senate race is lingering in an appeals court, with briefs not scheduled for weeks. And a win there for Democrats would only boost the party’s clinched majority. Counting was still underway Wednesday, with no clear winner.

Officials are ramping up an investigation in Alaska, where Attorney General Todd Blanche has said the apparent recruitment of a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, constituted “fraud on the ballot.”

Elias, a prolific election lawyer and outspoken Trump critic who was reportedly among those subpoenaed in the probe, said he expected to soon face Republican lawyers and the DOJ in court.

“These fights won’t affect control of Congress, but they will determine how much room Democrats have to maneuver in both chambers,” he said in an email to supporters Wednesday. “They will also set the stage for real oversight of, and accountability for, a president who has so far operated without either."

Officials have also subpoenaed California election officials, at least two of whom were scheduled to appear before a grand jury in Los Angeles on Wednesday morning in the DOJ’s investigation of purported voter registration and voting by noncitizens.

There’s also a possibility of recounts or candidate lawsuits arising in elections where counting is still underway and results remain close, including the Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska.

“We just don't know what the final margin is going to be and what the candidate who's behind is going to try to do,” David Becker, a former attorney in the DOJ's Voting Section who now heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research. “That's not election denialism. This is a legitimately close election.”

Beyond that, Becker said he anticipates that many of the ongoing cases between the DOJ and election officials or Democratic-led states will be dismissed, in part because the administration does not want to be held to the scrutiny that future discovery will require.

Any dismissals by the DOJ, Becker said, would “lay bare that this was a political strategy and not a law enforcement strategy.”

entries.title: Janeese Lewis George Unveils Mayoral Transition Team: ‘This is the Big Leagues’
entries.summary: She said operational competence and representation for all eight wards were prioritized over ideological alignment.
entries.content:
D.C. Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George formally launched her transition Wednesday, unveiling a roster of local government veterans, labor leaders and federal appointees tasked with building out her “people-first” administration.

Based at an office at 899 North Capitol St. NE, the transition will be directed by Jennifer Levy, who previously served as the first deputy attorney general in New York. Levy is flanked by five co-chairs: former D.C. Deputy Mayor Beatriz “BB” Otero, former White House Office of Presidential Personnel Director Gautam Raghavan, labor leader Greg Akerman, D.C. Action Executive Director Kimberly Perry and Aaron Jenkins, who served as President Barack Obama’s director of the Center for Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships.

The group will immediately begin vetting candidates for deputy mayors, agency directors and commissioners, accepting applications through a new jobs portal. On Wednesday, Lewis George emphasized that her transition leaders were selected based on their diverse range of experience and their ability to help her “prepare and deliver on Day 1.”

She said that operational competence and a commitment to representing all of the city’s eight wards were prioritized over pure ideological alignment.

“This is the big leagues,” Lewis George told reporters at the National Press Club in Washington. “It’s a group that I trust, and I hope that this shows residents of the District of Columbia that that’s where our government is headed, with credible, quality leaders who are ready to deliver on Day 1.”

Lewis George said a major priority for the team is ensuring no interruption in essential services, such as trash collection and snow removal, during the handover from Mayor Muriel Bowser’s administration.

Before overhauling the government structure, the transition team will conduct a “forensic analysis” of the city’s agencies and budget to identify efficiencies and savings, she said. She also floated the possibility of “desk audits" at some agencies to determine exactly what roles government employees are filling.

While she declined to go into specifics about how the city’s agencies and government leadership positions might change under her administration, she confirmed she will retain an economic development office — seeking a leader who can cut red tape for businesses, collaborate with the education and medical sectors and push toward her ambitious goal of building 72,000 homes.

Lewis George announced a contract with the Police Executive Research Forum to conduct a “national and local search” for the city’s next chief of police; she noted the independent organization has assisted with more than 200 police executive searches, including in Baltimore and Boston. Jeffery Carroll has served as interim police chief since December 2025.

“We will be making critical decisions over the next year or more to get our government where it needs to be,” she said.

Lewis George said her team is working on setting a meeting with President Donald Trump, adding that she sees an opportunity to work with him on shared priorities that benefit District residents, like the expansion of Union Station and federal transfers that provide the city with more land. She also aims to work with Congress to fully fund D.C. Superior Court, which would allow for the hiring of more magistrate judges — alleviating backlogs in criminal and landlord-tenant proceedings.

Lewis George said she will officially resign her Ward 4 D.C. Council seat the same day she is sworn in on Jan. 2, expressing hope that a special election to fill the vacancy will be held as soon as March 16. She also doubled down on campaign promises to release an accountability scorecard outlining resident feedback before she takes the oath of office.

Funding for the transition and an upcoming “people’s inauguration” will rely on council-allocated funds and small-dollar fundraising — barring corporate donations from entities currently doing business with the District.
