entries.title: Trump ‘Loves the Guy’: Sergio Gor Is In Line for a Top Job Post-Midterms
entries.summary: Currently the U.S. ambassador to India, Gor has been mentioned in Trump and State Department circles, as many predict an administration reshuffling.
entries.content:
Attention in Washington, D.C., is turning to who will rise in President Donald Trump's administration after Republicans endured a midterms thrashing Tuesday night. One name keeps surfacing: Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India.

Gor, a former top White House aide and close Trump ally, has been laying the groundwork for a major promotion in the aftermath of the midterm elections, according to 10 people familiar with internal conversations.

Well-connected, with direct access to Trump, Gor has had growing involvement in high-level meetings that’s given him influence well beyond his ambassadorship. He’s seen as a key power broker between Washington and much of Asia, and as a confidante to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The former head of the White House’s Office of Presidential Personnel maintains relationships across the Trump administration, having played a key role in the vetting and appointment of thousands of officials.

Now, Gor is being discussed in Trump’s circles as a candidate for senior administration positions for the second half of the president’s term. There’s also a widespread and rapidly circulating understanding among State Department officials that Gor is interested in such a promotion.

“He wants more of a forward-facing role,” said a U.S. official familiar with internal discussions.

Sources familiar with internal conversations said they’ve heard Gor’s name come up as a possibility for a number of powerful jobs, including White House chief of staff and taking over for Rubio as Secretary of State.

Neither Rubio nor White House chief of staff Susie Wiles have publicly indicated any intention of leaving the administration. Still, some at State and in Republican political circles believe Rubio may leave the Cabinet to prepare for a future run for president in 2028 or 2032. Wiles’ position is also widely seen as at risk in Trump’s orbit.

Some of the sources said Gor would also be interested in a different promotion within the State Department, such as replacing Deputy Secretary Chris Landau. Landau has told colleagues he would leave after the midterms if Republicans lost control of Congress, in anticipation of grueling investigations, according to a source who heard the comment.

Gor denied that he has any interest in another job and said he never discussed taking another role with anyone.

“This story is complete and total bullshit,” Gor told The Washington Sun. “Secretary Marco Rubio has proven to be the most qualified, accomplished and greatest secretary of state in history. He is irreplaceable, and a dear friend who I have the joy of working with every day as U.S. ambassador to India — a true honor of a lifetime. I have zero interest in any other role.”

Dylan Johnson, State’s assistant secretary for global public affairs, also denied that Gor is looking for a new role.

“Secretary Rubio and Ambassador Gor have a great working relationship and personal friendship,” Johnson said. “These are made-up rumors from anonymous sources. We look forward to revisiting this ‘reporting’ in a few weeks when it is revealed as the baseless fake news that it is.”

A White House official called the story “fake” and based on sources who “know nothing."

“Ambassador Gor has no interest in any other role and believes both Susie Wiles and Secretary Marco Rubio are doing a phenomenal job,” the official said.

Gor’s access to Trump and expanding diplomatic portfolio has raised his profile beyond India. The president "loves the guy,” a Trump adviser told The Sun. “He was the one guy in the wilderness years who was bringing him deals instead of asking for things."

As ambassador, Gor has helped facilitate a series of high-level visits to India, including by Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, and he’s used his dual role as ambassador and special envoy to participate in meetings with senior foreign officials outside India, including Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

"Ambassador Gor appears at times to be functioning as a deputy secretary," said Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. "It's good for India; he has helped turn around the relationship a lot because he has a direct line to the White House."

Rubio has visited India twice this year. The two men also appeared side by side in Atlanta at a G20 summit last week, and they’ve traveled together frequently since Gor’s appointment.

A second current State Department official described Gor as “giddy for the limelight” during major international events. The officials cited in this story spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.

Gor was central to Rubio’s trip to Uzbekistan last month, part of a Trump administration effort to draw the U.S. closer to Central Asian countries with significant natural resources. He was born in the country when it was part of the Soviet Union (a fact he previously declined to acknowledge), and in addition to being ambassador, he serves as a U.S. special envoy for South and Central Asia.

Two sources familiar with Gor's leadership said he reflects Trump's approach to foreign affairs, noting he is hyper-focused on dealmaking and heavily involved in supporting U.S. businesses. In Central Asia, one U.S. official said, “It’s easy to play there and get deliverables because of how the Central Asians play. It’s very transaction-based."

Trump’s sons are involved in a company planning to tap reserves of tungsten, a valuable metal, in Kazakhstan, whose leader Gor brought to the White House for a meeting with Trump and other Central Asian heads of state.

Gor, a Trump campaign aide in 2024, has previously been tied to the business interests of the president’s family. He publishes Trump’s books through his company and is particularly close with Donald Trump Jr. President Trump hosted a swearing-in ceremony for Gor in the Oval Office before the ambassador left for India, calling Gor a “great guy” and saying he was “very proud” of him.

In Delhi, where has served since November 2025, Gor has led the embassy with an unusual degree of control, according to two people familiar with the operations there. Gor has pushed out both career State employees and locally employed staff, and has gotten involved in all levels of personnel decisions in a manner not typical for an ambassador at an embassy of that size.

He also made waves when he canceled an $850 million construction project at the Delhi embassy after the first Trump administration had already broken ground for the overhaul.

Earlier this year, Rubio told The New York Times Gor’s “access to the president” made him “an enormous asset for both the host country and for us at the State Department.”

Whether those connections would be enough to land Gor a potential Senate-confirmed Cabinet position is less clear. Every Democrat voted against his ambassadorial confirmation as part of a larger package of nominees.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, suggested Gor's choices have displeased lawmakers and deserve scrutiny in a statement to The Sun. "Our embassy reflects our relationship with India, and cancelling the new Chancery in Delhi does not reflect the depth and breadth of our strong bilateral relationship, which has broad bipartisan support in Congress," said Meeks, who will likely chair the committee in the new Congress starting in January. "I intend to closely examine how the Department threw away more than half a billion dollars without informing Congress, as well as the role of Special Envoys who have been operating without accountability.”

Gor previously worked for about a decade on Capitol Hill, primarily for Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky). At the White House personnel office, Gor was responsible for identifying and vetting candidates for thousands of political appointment roles across government. While there, he publicly clashed with then-Trump adviser Elon Musk.

entries.title: Janeese Lewis George is D.C.’s Mayor-Elect. Here’s What Comes Next.
entries.summary: She made big promises and faces bigger obstacles, but a Democratic Congress is one less thing to worry about.
entries.content:
“Tonight our campaign ends,” said D.C. mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George to a crowd of cheering supporters on Tuesday night, only minutes after the D.C. Board of Elections confirmed her victory. “Tomorrow our work begins.”

Lewis George, a self-identified democratic socialist who easily bested a more well-established centrist candidate in June’s Democratic primary, has made political waves in D.C. this year and in the process brought to an end the 12 years of Mayor Muriel Bowser’s business-friendly rule over the city.

But she will also enter the mayor’s office facing significant challenges, from D.C.’s slumping economy and a looming fiscal cliff to relations with a mercurial president who has found that the most control he can easily wield is over the nation’s capital.

Lewis George launched her formal transition on Wednesday morning, a two-month sprint where her team will have to staff an administration and prepare for the Jan. 2 takeover. Here’s what she’s facing — both good and bad — as she ends her campaign and begins her work.

The List Of Challenges Is Long

If Tuesday night was for celebrating, Wednesday morning could well be for considering the “scaries.”

That’s how one council member told me they’re referring to the significant and scary budget realities Lewis George will assume immediately upon taking office. She’ll be tossed directly into the formulation of the city’s budget for 2028, and the numbers are already looking rough: Lewis George could face a budget deficit of anywhere from $650 to $850 million that she’ll have to close somehow, whether by raising additional revenue or cutting spending. And that’s just to sustain current levels of spending, not implement any of her own ambitious plans.

Some of those very plans, in fact, are wrapped up in that budget hole. Take the Pay Equity Fund, the $62.7 million annual pot of money that’s used to increase salaries for child care workers. Lewis George has championed it, but it’s currently budgeted to have no money after the current fiscal year. That means that Lewis George — who campaigned on making child care more affordable for all residents — will have to find money somewhere for it.
Voss-JLGwatchparty_40.jpg (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)The same goes for maintaining the city’s existing child care subsidy program, which she has said she wants to expand so that it eventually covers all families regardless of income. The subsidy program faces a $50 million hit next year, and that doesn’t even include what it would cost to start expanding it.

The difficult spending decisions will also cut directly at the coalition that led her to victory. Dozens of labor unions representing some 10,000 D.C. government workers are agitating for a new contract that guarantees them cost-of-living increases that they’ve largely foregone for the last year — and could go without for the next four. While teachers, police officers and firefighters have all recently gotten new contracts and raises, there’s currently no money in the budget to extend the same to the other unions.

And that’s just the beginning. Lewis George will have to find ways to kickstart D.C.’s slumping economy after federal layoffs and related cuts that have cost the city more 36,000 jobs, while weighing that against her promises to raise taxes on wealthy residents and close loopholes that benefit law firms and lobbying shops.

Still, the size of those challenges doesn’t dissuade her supporters from thinking she can still be a successful executive.

“We know politicians aren’t magicians,” said Kurtis Hagans, chair of the Metro D.C. Democratic Socialists of America, in an interview with The Washington Sun. “We know JLG will be limited by a budget and an anti-Janeese president, but she still has control over the office in terms of how she gets the message out to Washingtonians.”

The Opportunities Could Come in Starting Small

Lewis George herself isn’t blind to the challenges she faces, and on Tuesday night she said that being a democratic socialist mayor of D.C. won’t just be about the big swings — but also the smaller ones that residents might notice more quickly.

“We will pick up the trash, plow the snow, eliminate the rats, and make it easier to open a small business and easier to keep it open,” she said. (To that end, last month she pledged to create a new position of D.C. rat czar.)
Voss-JLGwatchparty_30 (1).jpg (5561x3708, AR: 1.50)Voss-JLGwatchparty_25.jpg (8471x5647, AR: 1.50)That focus on the nuts-and-bolts of running D.C. has unified seemingly disparate factions of the city’s politics.

“Nobody elected you to be Secretary of State. They elected you to take care of potholes. That’s true for the mayor and true for the council. We’re not here to solve all the world’s problems,” said former mayor Anthony Williams in an interview with Capital Commonsense this week.

Lewis George has also said that she wants to dig into current spending by city agencies, both to root out waste and find ways to control spending.

A Democratic Congress Makes Life Much Easier For JLG

Lewis George may be facing local challenges to her ambitious platform, but with Tuesday’s midterm elections now settled, at least Capitol Hill won’t be one.

Over the last two years the Republican-led House Oversight Committee has been a thorn in D.C.’s side, introducing, debating and passing multiple bills that touched on everything from the city’s criminal justice policies to whether traffic cameras should be permitted. Most stalled in the Senate, but the message from the Hill was clear: We’re watching, and we have power over you.

With Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) set to take over the committee, the congressional interference isn’t only expected to stop, but it could well be reversed. “We will remove every budget rider on DC next year and pass DC statehood in 2029,” wrote shadow Senator Ankit Jain on X.

Statehood still faces challenges in the Senate, but Jain’s invocation of budget riders is significant. Those are Republican-sponsored provisions that are dropped into the federal budget targeting specific D.C. policies and practices. The city has been banned from legalizing recreational marijuana for more than a decade, for example, and isn’t allowed to spend any of its local funds on subsidizing abortions for low-income women. It’s likely that Democrats could remove those two riders.

Coupled with that, Lewis George will benefit from her close relationship with Robert White, D.C.’s incoming delegate, and she’s pledged to walk the halls of Congress more than Bowser did.
2026-11-3 Midterm Election Coverage Robert White (2840x1894, AR: 1.50)But Trump Remains Unpredictable

If navigating Congress will be easier for Lewis George, the already challenging relationship she has with President Donald Trump could get even more complicated — and in unexpected ways.

The two are already starting from a point of friction. Trump has derided Lewis George as a “communist” and mused about taking over D.C. should she cross unstated lines. For her part, Lewis George has pledged that on the first day of her term she will end cooperation between the Metropolitan Police Department and immigration agents that Trump has deployed across the city.

Trump, of course, still retains plenty of power over D.C. In August 2025 he proved as much when he federalized MPD for a month and deployed the National Guard. He’s also gone on a renovation streak across D.C., fixing up parks and fountains (which many locals have appreciated) and obsessing over the Reflecting Pool and building a new golf course at East Potomac Park (which plenty of residents don’t love).

In fact, Trump’s interest in fixing up D.C. seems to have increased as he lost control over some national and international events; with Congress now going to the Democrats, doing more renovating may be the last thing he can do somewhat unimpeded.

On Tuesday, though, Lewis George again said that she’s not solely looking for conflict with Trump. “I'm willing to meet with the president. I'm looking forward to talking about how we can work together to benefit D.C. residents,” she said after casting her ballot. (New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani did the same, much to his benefit.)

“To me, it's just about being strategic and working with your partners, and finding the things we do agree on, and double down on those things,” she said.

entries.title: Richard Hudson Conceded — And It Gets Worse for North Carolina Republicans
entries.summary: “It’s hard to think of a better poster child for the Democratic wave” than the NRCC chair going down, a Democratic strategist said.
entries.content:
Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, spent his birthday on Wednesday conceding to his Democratic opponent.

It’s a loss that captures just how badly the election went for Hudson’s party, given that he was tasked with defending the Republican majority in the House.

“God is sovereign over my life, and He has a plan for all of us,” Hudson said in a statement. “In the words of Ronald Reagan: we lost a skirmish, but the battle goes on.”

His loss emphasized the major gains made by Democrats: Republicans drew Hudson’s district to be a safe-red seat in the 2024 election, which he won by 20 percentage points.

“It's hard to think of a better poster child for the Democratic wave than the chairman of the [NRCC] losing a district that was drawn to be impervious to Democratic waves,” Asher Hildebrand, a North Carolina Democratic strategist, told The Washington Sun.

The race was widely seen as solidly in Hudson’s favor, but his campaign reserved tens of thousands of dollars in TV ad buys in the district in early October in a tacit admission that he anticipated trouble in a national environment that favored Democrats.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee also targeted Hudson’s district on its optimistic “districts in play” list. Last month, the flagship Democratic House super PAC told donors that “more expansion seats,” including Hudson’s, were “within reach.”

Richard Ojeda, the Democrat on track to win Hudson’s seat, spent 24 years in the U.S. Army, including time at North Carolina’s Fort Bragg, which is in the district. He ran on a progressive platform, telling local TV station WXII that the United States should provide universal health care and forgive college student loans. Ojeda raised $2.9 million this cycle, lagging behind Hudson’s $4.2 million.

Hildebrand said Hudson’s loss may speak more to national trends than to the lawmaker’s own shortcomings.

“I can't point to a single misstep that Hudson has made other than the collective misstep that Republicans may have made by overestimating the broader environment in their favor,” Hildebrand said.

A year ago, North Carolina’s Republican-led Legislature once again redrew Democratic Rep. Don Davis’ congressional district with the intention of bringing “an additional Republican seat to the North Carolina congressional delegation,” as one state Republican lawmaker said at the time. Republicans hoped that the newest version of the map would give their party 11 of the state’s 14 seats, despite how competitive the state is more broadly.

Instead, Davis’ opponent conceded Tuesday night in what AdImpact called the most expensive House general election on record, and Democrats were on track to win as many as nine other House seats in the state. They also recaptured a U.S. Senate seat.

As of Wednesday evening, The Associated Press had yet to call 10 North Carolina U.S. House races, including Hudson's. But with the state reporting unofficial results from 100% of precincts, incumbent Republican Reps. Addison McDowell and Brad Knott conceded their races and Rep. Tim Moore appeared to be on track to lose.

At least four races could land within the 1% margin needed for a candidate to ask for a recount. Those were the races in the districts represented by Republican Reps. Virginia Foxx, Pat Harrigan, Greg Murphy and David Rouzer.

None of those races were widely considered competitive until Tuesday night. To many observers’ surprise, Democrats also won control of the state House and broke the GOP supermajority in the state Senate. That supermajority had previously allowed the Legislature to override the veto of enfeebled Democratic governors.

In an election night interview with CBS News, outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said Democrats didn’t win those races so much as Republicans lost them.

“I think probably the spreading out of some of our Republican base with redistricting, which I said was a bad idea … with this wave trend we see tonight, I think it's putting some what I thought were safer races, even in North Carolina, at risk, and that's unfortunate,” Tillis said.

Tillis did not run for reelection this year, and former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper handily defeated President Donald Trump’s chosen candidate, Michael Whatley, in the U.S. Senate race.

Democrats also won the two races that were anticipated to be competitive: Davis kept his seat and Jamie Ager was projected to defeat Jennifer Balkcom to flip Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards’ seat.

entries.title: Could a Democratic Wave Revive Immigration Reform?
entries.summary: The administration’s immigration crackdown generated backlash with voters that could change the conversation in Washington.
entries.content:
The stunning election sweep by Democrats seemingly thawed negotiations over immigration policy, one of the most contentious topics during President Donald Trump’s second term.

As it became clear Democrats would take control of the House and Senate, Trump struck a less strident tone than the aggressive approach to immigration enforcement that has defined his administration.

“We can work with them on immigration, I think. Immigration is a big deal. I’ve always felt we should be able to work on immigration,” Trump said on a call to Fox News.

Sen.-elect James Talarico, whose historic flip in Texas was supported by Latino voters, offered a similar take. “He has done a better job than the previous administration in securing our border, but we also need to create more legal pathways for hardworking immigrants who want to come here and contribute to our economy,” Talarico said during a Fox News interview Wednesday morning.

The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has led to the killings of immigrants and U.S. citizens, the detention of tens of thousands and the erasure of legal status for more than a million. Although immigration was not a top issue, including for Latinos, polls showed for months before the midterm elections that voters said Trump’s immigration enforcement strategy had gone too far.

Vice President JD Vance acknowledged in a post-election message that administration actions cost Republicans the legislative branch, mostly blaming the Iran war but also mentioning immigration. While he also voiced willingness for change, Vance remained closed off to granting legal status for undocumented immigrants.

“Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty,” Vance wrote in an X post. “I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.”

Democrats in committees dealing with immigration see an opportunity for change.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California), ranking member of the Senate Judiciary subcommittee on immigration issues, said in a statement Wednesday that it’s time to “get to work.”

Padilla said he wants to pass legislation granting a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for years and paid taxes. “Yesterday, the American people showed up and demanded a better future,” he said. “Now it’s Congress’ job to build it.”

His counterpart in the House, Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), said Trump’s attacks on immigrants created momentum for reforms like citizenship for people who came into the country as minors, or the spouses, kids and parents of Americans.

“So I do think that there's a chance that our humane immigration reform legislation could get support in the Senate and that we could send it to the president’s desk,” Jayapal said. “Whether or not he signs it is a whole other issue.”

More than 60% of Latino voters supported Democratic candidates in House and Senate races, according to a new poll from BSP Research and the African American Research Collaborative commissioned by a slew of immigrant rights groups. The poll, conducted between Oct. 20 and Election Day, showed 63% of Latinos worried they would be targeted by government policies because of their race, ethnicity, religion, language, immigration status or national origin.

House Democrats were quick to reinforce their intentions to investigate immigration agents’ abuse of power and Department of Homeland Security operations. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California), who is set to become the chair of the House Oversight Committee, in an X post as the blue tsunami materialized Tuesday night, gave a two-word warning: “Lawyer up.”

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi), ranking member of the House Homeland Security Committee, said he is preparing to probe DHS’s standards for hiring immigration agents, training and enforcement policies and sole-source contracts.

Thompson said he remains skeptical of the Trump administration’s willingness for a bipartisan agreement on the issue but that he is looking forward to civil conversations.

“When you get your head handed to you on a silver platter, and some of your policies have contributed to that occurring, I’m certain that it has a humbling effect,” Thompson told The Washington Sun. “But I remain to see if, for once during his presidency on immigration, that Donald Trump tells the truth.”

Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois) posted on social media that current and former immigration officials in the Trump administration should clear their calendars to deal with congressional oversight efforts over the next two years.

But Democrats’ plans for oversight investigations are all but certain to face opposition from the Trump administration.

“It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing,” DHS general counsel James Percival posted in response to Ramirez. “Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland,” Percival said on X.

entries.title: Republicans Redistricted to Win More Seats. They Won Almost None of Them.
entries.summary: The congressional map race ended in a near wash amid the midterms’ blue wave. Republicans running in districts they made to be more party friendly fell to Democrats.
entries.content:
Republicans across the country rushed over the last 18 months to redraw their state’s congressional maps to make districts more favorable to their party at President Donald Trump’s urging. The party had hoped to net approximately 15 seats to hold on to its House majority.

But, as votes are tallied from Texas to Florida to Alabama, the redraws are on track to end in a wash.

In Alabama, Democrat Rep. Shomari Figures is projected to hold on to a seat that state Republicans tried to draw him out of after the Supreme Court gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in April. In Florida, Democrats were projected to win three — and possibly one more — of the four districts that Republicans had carved up.

In North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District — which became the most expensive House race in U.S. history, according to AdImpact — Rep. Don Davis has a strong lead to hold on to his seat thanks in part to a blue wave that hit North Carolina particularly hard.

And in Texas, the state that set off the redistricting spree, GOP candidates likely lost four of the five seats their new map was aimed at flipping.

“Make no mistake about it: Republicans drew our congressional maps to steal five seats from the people of Texas,” Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party, told The Washington Sun on Wednesday. “Instead of gaining five seats, they are now going to be losing seats in Texas.”

In Tennessee, which was redrawn to ultimately split Memphis into three congressional districts, Democratic nominee and state Rep. Justin Pearson did not concede until Wednesday afternoon in a race where he was trailing by just over 1 percentage point. But in Tennessee’s 4th District, a race that was rated “solid Republican” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, now has a Democrat in the lead with 99% of the vote counted.

Another state where Republicans redrew the lines was Louisiana, which held the district at the center of the Louisiana v. Callais Supreme Court case. Those races were too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon, showing Democrats holding up even in districts that were favorable — sometimes by double digits — to their opponents using 2024 presidential margins. Those races are likely headed to a recount.

In California, where Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom led Proposition 50 in an effort to net his party up to five more congressional seats, Democrats are projected to pick up at least four of them — and are looking likely to pick up the last one, too.

Democrats have been pushing back on Republican redraw efforts in their own ways, including by redrawing in California, ballot propositions and legal mechanisms. But, John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said the overwhelming Democratic wins were “a complete rebuke” of Republican redistricting efforts.

“What this took to happen was Donald Trump standing in front of the American people and saying, ‘I acknowledge that I cannot win on fair lines. I acknowledge that my ideas are going to be so toxic that I need to cheat more than I already have in order to hold the House of Representatives,’ and that’s rare,” Bisognano said.

Adam Kincaid, the executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust, said the redistricting that his party launched was a firewall against Republicans losing even more seats in states like Texas. But, he said, the night was still dire.

“I told a lot of people going into the night that it could be anything from bad to kind of OK to apocalyptic,” Kincaid said. “We got apocalyptic.”

In North Carolina, when the race at the top of the ticket — the Senate contest between Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley — began turning toward Cooper, Kincaid said he began to get nervous about the outcome.

“When the North Carolina Senate race stopped being competitive, I just got really worried about all of those districts,” he continued. “I was hoping that wasn't going to happen, but with the environment being as bad as it was, it washed all of them out.”

Bisognano said that, especially when considered in the context of not just the state’s 2025 redraw but also the change to the maps in 2022, the North Carolina outcome and races like Figures’ in Alabama showed that voters were tuned in and responded.

“North Carolina is a place that understands redistricting, having all of the egregious gerrymandering happen to it over the course of the past 10 years,” Bisognano said. The state, he said, “reached a boiling point where they were ready to come out and really vote at a rate that no one expected.”

Democrats also came out on top in a slew of ballot measures about redistricting.

In Missouri, voters rejected a proposition that would have put in place a Republican-friendly map for future elections. In Maryland, voters approved a ballot measure that would open the door for Democrats to more easily redraw their maps as early as next year. And in Colorado, a Republican-led measure aimed at making it harder for Democrats to redistrict seemed on track to fail as of Wednesday afternoon.

Both parties are already looking ahead to see what states will pick up the pen ahead of 2028. On Wednesday morning, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican, announced that his state would not redraw after it elected a Democratic senator and governor, saying that “the voters of our state have spoken.”

"Gov. Kemp saying that he's not going to redraw I think is quite a savvy move in that this is a completely toxic issue,” Bisognano said. “Donald Trump took it on head-on, believed at his core, seemingly, that no one cared, and was proven so deeply wrong."

entries.title: House Republicans Have No Clue Who Will Lead Them
entries.summary: Two current members of leadership are running for the top spots but their challengers argue it’s time for a change.
entries.content:
After Tuesday’s election massacre, the House Republican Conference is in chaos and it’s now an open question of who will lead it in the next Congress.

Next Tuesday, House Republicans will decide who will take the reins in the top two leadership spots. Speaker Mike Johnson informed his staff on Wednesday morning that he does not plan to run for the top Republican spot again, clearing the way for a rematch between House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) and House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) for minority leader, the two announced candidates in the race.

Both men had begun laying the groundwork for their respective runs ahead of the midterms but both lost many of their key allies to Tuesday’s blue tsunami, leaving the race without a clear frontrunner.

The No. 2 spot to be the minority whip looked to be House Majority Whip Tom Emmer’s for the taking. Going into Tuesday night the consensus among members was that Emmer (R-Minnesota) wouldn’t have a challenger unless the night went very badly.

And it went very badly.

Almost immediately on Wednesday morning, Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) released a dear colleague announcing his intentions to run for whip against Emmer, who also announced his bid.

This year’s leadership election will focus on two key questions: Who does the conference trust to lead them in the minority and who will be able to pick up the pieces to deliver a majority in 2028?

Scalise bested Jordan in 2023 on a private ballot for speaker during the drawn out fight following then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy’s ouster — in the end neither could get the 218 votes necessary to become speaker. Then, it was a snap election while Republicans were actively in the majority. This year, Republicans will be voting with the midterm blowout still fresh on their minds.

Both Scalise and Jordan released “Dear Colleague” letters on Wednesday to make their case.

Scalise emphasized that he has a history of leading and already has the political infrastructure in place to help retake the majority in 2028.

“My number one goal as Republican Leader will be to win back the majority and I expect you to hold me accountable to that mission,” he said in the letter. “To succeed, we will need to be effective in both the oversight and legislative fights ahead, but we will also need to lay out a clear and optimistic vision for America.”

Jordan talked up his prowess for combatting Democratic investigations, which are inevitable next Congress.

“Democrats have already signaled their true intentions. Each Democrat-led committee will turn their full attention to investigating every facet of the administration and private entities across the country,” Jordan said. “I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook. I know what it will take to lead our conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the democrats' tactics. We need a leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting.”

The two have been working the phones calling members pitching themselves for the position, sources say.

Those close to Scalise argue that he should lead the conference because of his track record dating back more than a decade in helping elect and recruit Republicans to run.

Those close to Jordan and others in the conference argue that after Tuesday’s gargantuan losses there should be a complete repudiation of current leadership.

Emmer and his team have spent most of the day Wednesday making calls to members pitching why he should remain as whip.

Part of that pitch includes how he helped take back the majority as National Republican Congressional Committee chair in 2020 and 2022 following the 2018 wipeout, a source told The Washington Sun.

In a dear colleague letter, Emmer emphasized this point.

“When I took over the NRCC in 2019, we needed to change. We needed to install a winning culture. In 2020, we were expected to lose up to 24 seats,” Emmer said in the letter. “We fought tooth and nail, and gained a historic 15 seats, nearly flipping the House in a presidential year. In 2022, we finished the job. We've taken on the tough fights as a team, and won. We must return to that same mindset to retake the majority in two years.”

He added that if reelected as whip he would “continue to be direct, honest, and transparent. We have never made false promises or tried to buy your votes. My role is to support every Member of this conference and help you succeed. Success will feel different in the minority-and often less satisfying-but will require no less support and unity in our conference.”

His opponent, Pfluger, is taking a path similar to Jordan and hoping to ride the wave of anti-leadership sentiment in his bid to unseat Emmer.

“It is time to regroup, recharge, and fully unify,” Pfluger said in his letter. “We need fresh ideas and a leadership team committed to rebuilding a culture with a clear game plan to win in 2028. I’m running for Republican Whip because I believe that I am capable and can be trusted to implement the changes this team needs.”

As for the members who will be voting on these positions, it’s the current GOP leadership who they think is in the hot seat.

“I would hate to be a member of current leadership,” one senior GOP member told The Sun on Tuesday night.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: It’s the War, Stupid
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Nov. 4, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

President Donald Trump gathered the press this afternoon to talk not about Republicans’ historic midterm losses but instead the marble he’s sourcing for the White House ballroom.

In response to questions, he acknowledged a lengthy post from JD Vance that blamed the war in Iran for Republicans’ coast-to-coast drubbing (Vance didn’t sound very supportive of the war effort).

  • The New York Post declared the diatribe Vance’s “Hillbilly Eulogy.” The Washington Sun’s Igor Bobic reports that Republican lawmakers and commentators are downgrading Vance’s 2028 odds after yesterday’s shellacking. 
  • It’s still early, but Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis appear poised to gain the most from this new leadership vacuum, Igor reports. 
The great GOP shakeup is here. As Democrats’ blue wave crashes into Washington, new Republican leaders are finding their footing in its wake. Mike Johnson will step down as party leader, but outgoing Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan and Majority Leader Steve Scalise have already thrown their hats into the ring to replace him.

  • Trump said today that he would “stay out of” the race.




THE ADMINISTRATION

Who’s in? Attention is turning to who will rise in Trump’s administration after last night’s bruising. One name keeps surfacing: Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India.

Who’s out? Trump is asking advisers whether he should get rid of Pete Hegseth, CBS News reported.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

As for pending results, we’re still waiting on Senate and gubernatorial counts out of Alaska, as well as the incredibly tight Mississippi Senate race. Results from both could take days to finalize.

  • Chuck Schumer has deployed DSCC officials to Mississippi to make sure every vote is counted. 




THE HILL

Jockeying has begun for more positions of power inside Congress:

  • Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) has launched a bid for House minority whip.
  • Freshman Rep. Brian Jack (R-Georgia) says he’s ready to pick up the NRCC mantle after the shocking defeat of Rep. Richard Hudson (R-North Carolina). 
  • Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Michigan) announced she will run for reelection as House Republican Conference chair. 
Democrats also aren’t waiting to put themselves in line for top party posts. Hakeem Jeffries made it official: he’s running for speaker. And Schumer appeared bullish about being reelected the top Senate Democrat, despite facing his own impending intra-party wave of candidates who vowed not to support him.

  • “The issue is not me,” he told reporters today. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader.”
Republicans’ reconciliation dreams have not yet been dashed, MS NOW reports. GOP lawmakers are exploring a last-ditch, catch-all legislative package that could include billions in Iran war funding, new voting laws, raising the debt ceiling and even hemp policies before Democrats take control in January.





THE STATES

Georgia’s congressional maps are here to stay. Gov. Brian Kemp rebuffed calls from fellow Republicans to hold a special, lame-duck session to redraw the maps.

entries.title: Midterm Voters Reject Data Centers
entries.summary: The results could set up a new wave of state policy on data center guardrails.
entries.content:
It was a bad night for data centers.

In hotly contested gubernatorial races, Democrats who campaigned on pausing development beat Republican challengers who proposed more moderate approaches. At least 38 towns and cities passed ballot measures to restrict data centers locally.

The message voters sent was clear even to Elon Musk, who appeared to be writing off the future of data centers on Earth as results rolled in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he posted on X on election night.

Americans’ strong opposition to data centers, and by extension the results of Tuesday’s elections, could have a real impact on the future of the industry. Some artificial intelligence industry stocks fell as investors contended with political shifts in states that host large swaths of planned development. The decisive swing toward Democrats in several states could allow governors and state legislatures to move quickly on state policy that places new regulations on AI infrastructure developers, restricting the massive growth they’ve pursued over the past two years.

An analysis from Cleanview Energy, a company that tracks U.S. power infrastructure and data center development, shows 41% of the country's data centers could be paused.

“I think data centers were just right at that nexus of both the cost and corruption issues that people cited in exit polls as their top two issues,” said Jesse Lee, a senior adviser at Climate Power, an advocacy group.

Lee called Tuesday’s results a “huge repudiation” of the data center build-out that has happened throughout the Trump administration. Democrats should start from scratch and reimagine an approach to data center policy that gives communities “a real say,” he said.

In Texas, Georgia and Ohio, Democrats who ran on data center moratoria won tough gubernatorial races. Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford, who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, ran on pausing tax abatements and incentives and opposing data centers on public lands.

Democrats also won control of state governments in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and likely Arizona. Lena Moffitt, executive director of the advocacy group Evergreen Action, said those blue sweeps have given state officials the power to deliver on promises to lower energy costs using clean energy.

“A lot of that is going to look like data center accountability, utility accountability, and I think they’re going to move fast and strong on those things,” she said.

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa made data centers a major part of her race against Gov. Greg Abbott, putting out a set of priorities that included stopping data center companies from using nondisclosure agreements, requiring union labor, and stopping subsidies.

She hit Abbott on his 2015 signing of a law that allowed for 20-year tax breaks for data center developers.

Abbott reversed course in August, announcing a pause on data center approvals and an audit of the way those projects were handling water, power and community impacts. Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was trounced by James Talarico in the first Senate election in Texas that has gone blue in decades, also tried to get in on the action, issuing letters to push data centers to provide that information.

But those actions seem to have fallen flat for voters in a state where more than 80% said they were concerned about the impact data centers could have on the cost and quality of living and 79% support limiting the number of data centers that can be built, according to a survey from the University of Houston.

Hinojosa told ABC News that data centers reflect a larger problem voters have with longtime politicians, calling it a “physical manifestation” of a governor “doing the bidding of the moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves.”

For hyperscalers in that state, which accounts for about 26% of the country’s planned data center capacity, the stakes are high.

“It’s certainly not a great outcome for developers who were looking to build huge AI facilities and things sort of largely unchecked,” said Abhi Rajendran, a nonresident fellow at the Center for Energy Studies at Rice University.

Rajendran said Texas could back out of “heavy deregulation,” and even a modest regulatory environment could represent a big change.

Georgia’s Democratic governor-elect, Keisha Lance Bottoms, has also pushed for a pause on data center development. Her opponent, Republican health care executive Rick Jackson, focused throughout his campaign on the way local communities could benefit from data center development — a sentiment that hews close to President Donald Trump’s approach to data centers.

Trump has said communities that welcome data centers are “smart,” while calling those that reject AI infrastructure “backwards and poor.”

Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy also focused on the economic benefits of data centers, writing an op-ed in The Columbus Dispatch over the summer that advertised free electricity and slashed taxes under his data center plan.

He lost to Democrat Amy Acton, who cast Ramaswamy as a friend of “big-tech billionaires.” Acton has supported a conditional moratorium on data centers to ensure they cover their costs, build with union labor on brownfields and previously industrial sites where jobs have been lost, and operate transparently and under state environmental laws.

Michigan’s Democratic governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson, pushed for a moratorium until the state creates rules forcing AI infrastructure developers to negotiate with communities and pay for power, among other guardrails.

Tom Lenard, Michigan director at Climate Power, said Tuesday’s result amounted to a rejection of Trump’s agenda and alignment with big tech.

“The people of Michigan chose Jocelyn Benson in this election because they know she will work for an affordable future that includes access to cheaper, cleaner energy,” he said.

With these wins, the policy environment in key states where data center developers are trying to scale up quickly could become even more important in the coming months.

“Particularly if we don’t fix the stuff at the federal level, then the data center debate comes down to a bunch of states,” said Abe Silverman, an assistant research scholar at Johns Hopkins.

Silverman said despite the “crazy level of rhetorical bipartisan consensus” that data centers need to pay their own way, there’s been a major lack of real policy implementation. For states, making those rules will require guts, he said.

“That really requires some very bold leadership at the state level to make those kinds of hard choices, given the political power of the data center industry and the interest in the labor community in building data centers and the economic development imperatives and everything else,” he said.
